speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BROADCASTING, FILMS AND ASSISTANCE TO THE ARTS CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order, please. Yesterday the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) sought to move concurrence in the report of the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts. The Chair expressed reservations about a procedural aspect of the report, more particularly in relation to the form of the recommendation of the committee. I undertook to look into the matter more closely. It now appears that the French language text of the report was correct as to form. The chairman has agreed to make the necessary correction to the English text so that the recommendations of the committee are now couched in the required words to the effect that the committee recommends that the government give consideration to the advisability of taking certain action. The hon. member may therefore proceed with the motion.

subtopic: BROADCASTING, FILMS AND ASSISTANCE TO THE ARTS CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
that the second report of the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, presented to the House on Monday, July 16, be now concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, there is an agreement that there will not be a debate on this motion and as chairman of the committee who put forward the motion it is my duty to make a mis au point with regard to the reporting of this matter in the press because of the importance of this subject. I would commend the body of the report not only to hon. members but also to the press because in it is contained the substance of what was discussed in the cpmmittee. It was the feeling of the committee that, although a complete ban on children's advertising would not be the route to follow, the CRTC will be asked to regulate in such a way that there will be no direct advertising exclusively aimed at children; in other words, that it be aimed at the parents. This is something that should be well understood because, although it was not possible for the committee to prove scientifically that there was actual harm to children, it was considered that an exploitation of children exists when advertising is directed to them, and this is not at all desirable.

I did not really have a chance to put forward many of my views on the report. I must say that the report which I finally saw covers many of the interesting points that were advanced in the testimony before the committee, but I cannot agree with what the chairman of the committee just said or what is set out in the report regarding the use of the word "exploitation". If we are to refer to exploitation in connection with advertising, depending on how exploitation is defined, we can say that there is exploitation in any and all forms of advertising.

speechtext:
What I do not like, Mr. Speaker, is the unseemly haste both in drawing up the committee report after a month's long debate, and in this move for concurrence today. I did not see any notice of any committee meeting, although the steering committee may have met and decided to move concurrence in the report today. But still I do not quite understand why the move has been made today.
If such a term as "exploitation of children" can be applied to television advertising, I would point out no one has a monopoly on children and on what happens to them with respect to television. I have four children myself. That does not quite tally with the numerals of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), but I would point out that children are exploited by their parents anyway, at least up to the ages of four or five, so that they may start to learn some of the guidelines laid down for adulthood. I do not believe that eliminating television advertising will necessarily be the cure for this problem. As a matter of fact, I think the committee missed a golden opportunity to put the CBC right on the spot. If it is to act as a public

July 24, 1973
Broadcasting Committee
network I do not believe there should be advertising on the state system. The state pays for that system.
We do not have a distinctive Canadian television system right now. Canadian radio is distinctive, but not television, and if we are ever to have a distinctive Canadian system I think we could have taken a small step forward by having no children's advertising. Let the state system be supplied with funds, either through underwriting or in some other way, to make up for the lost advertising dollar. That applies to the state system. Let the private network show advertisements, but only in conformity with the advertising code that we are told is going to be administered more strictly by the CRTC. Instead of that, Mr. Speaker, we have a hodgepodge in the recommendations contained in the report.
First, the CRTC in some mysterious way is supposed to define exploitation. Second, it is to have the almost impossible task of trying to define what advertising is geared to parents and what advertising is geared to children. I do not know how some of my hon. friends view the realities of the situation, but what of the program called "M-A-S-H"? Incidentally, that is a good word when one starts thinking of committee reports. M-A-S-H is sponsored by an advertiser, and is shown sometimes in the afternoon and sometimes at night. I suggest that children of six years and over, probably under 12 years, will look at this program if their parents let them, and are just as interested in M-A-S-H as they are in Bugs Bunny on Saturday mornings.
Take the case of the program "Man from U.N.C.L.E." or "Girl from U.N.C.L.E." which is shown from five to six o'clock in the afternoon. Mr. Speaker, I will certainly take the girl from U.N.C.L.E. any day, any way, and that program is supposed to be geared to the grey area between adulthood and childhood.

I suppose there are some very adult things in that program, yet the children seem to like it a lot. How in the world can the CRTC deal with that situation?
The Broadcasting Committee has not even touched the fundamental problem that it should be dealing with this session. A green paper on communications was filed by the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) three months ago. As I say, the Broadcasting Committee has not even touched it. The committee has dealt with advertising directed at children, something which is important and interesting. Some hon. members deserve a lot of credit for raising the subject, but I believe it has been raised out of all proportion to the fundamental problems of broadcasting and communications. Loading another element of responsibility on to the CRTC to help decide whether a program is designed for adults or children, and whether there is exploitation of children in advertisements, I think makes the work of the committee rather ridiculous. These are the remarks I should like to make now, even though the chairman said there is not supposed to be a debate.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Broadcasting Committee, I rise in support

of the motion for concurrence. I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member who just finished speaking. He admitted that he was not at the steering committee meeting, or the final broadcasting committee meeting, which drew up the recommendations. His comments obviously indicate his absence because most of them were directed at children's programming. That is not what the committee recommended; it recommended that advertising not be directed specifically at the child. We heard evidence that the child is too immature to make rational decisions on advertising that is designed primarily to make him act as a salesman or, although he has not the money, to make him pressure his parents into buying goods. We found that the child could not gain information from the 30 second or 50 second commercial which was mainly designed to pressure him into buying or to pressure parents into buying.
This is a sound recommendation which attempts to eliminate a serious problem in our society, a problem on which parents have expressed their concern to members of parliament. I would urge that all members of the House support this resolution that the committee has drawn up.

subtopic: BROADCASTING, FILMS AND ASSISTANCE TO THE ARTS CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not a member of the committee in question, but from what I hear, the report deals with advertising aimed at children, and which exploits adults as well as children.
It has just been said that it is not good for children to see such advertisements, and I would add that there are some fifty-year olds who have about as much sense as five-year olds. Television advertisements would be just as harmful to them, as to the children.
If agreement has been reached between the various political parties, within the committee, that the report be tabled without debate by the chairman, who is undoubtedly the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), I will raise no objection. Only it would be very important for the committee to take into account the attitude of the CRTC and the CBC.
It was said earlier that it would be acceptable if no advertisements were televised on the government network. I am in total agreement on this point. The national network, which is financed by the people of Canada, must at least spare us the moronic advertisements one sees all day long on the CBC.
Once again I say that I will raise no objection if agreement has already been reached that the committee report be tabled in this House without debate.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TAPS TANKER ROUTE-SUGGESTION CANADA RECOMMEND MOVING CHERRY POINT REFINERY FARTHER SOUTH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps this question gives me the opportunity to clarify a point that seems to be a bit obscure. The Canadian government's principal objection to the TAPS line proposal has to do with the possibility that large tanker's would enter the narrow waters of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. The question of whether the United States should build a pipeline across Alaska and carry oil down to California is not really a question upon which we have much of an opportunity to express a view. However, with respect to the narrow waters of the Strait of Juan de Fuca, I believe we have just as much interest as the United States. It is on this point we have centered our objections. I say to the hon. member if we could remove that problem, the rest is a matter that does not concern us directly.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister, both in that capacity and as Secretary of State for External Affairs. First, it is calling upon the Crown, in any charge which would be laid if this amendment became law, to prove that rape or attempted rape had been committed. This has to be established by evidence beyond any reasonable doubt, and as it involves a sexual offence of this type it has been held by the courts-although it is not in the written law of the country-that there must be corroboration in some material respect.
These are exceedingly difficult cases to prove. As I said last night, anybody involved in the professional career of law, either prosecuting or defending such cases, will realize this fact. In the event of the death of the poor unfortunate victim, the capacity for there to be corroborating evidence becomes exceedingly slim, if not impossible. Even if that offence is proved and having gone on to the next stage, you must then establish that the death of the person involved can be laid at the door of the person charged with the offence. I am only putting this forward, Mr. Speaker, not as a reason for not passing the amendment but simply to set out the problems and the difficulties which are conjured up by the hon. member's amendment. Indeed, it would probably require very substantial changes in the law of evidence if there is ever to be a conviction under this proposal of the hon. member.
There are others, of course, who say that such a provision constitutes a deterrence. There are elements of deterrence in the punishments which we have on our statute books, but from my experience I must say that in addition to deterrence there are substantial elements of fear and vengeance involved. I think these are not emotions which need be hidden. I do not say they are healthy emotions, but they exist, Mr. Speaker. Notwithstanding the progress of society over thousands of years, fear and vengeance are emotions which are still very much present in our society as a whole and in its individual members.
I understand these emotions. There is fear by parents about the perpetration of any of these horrible offences on their children. There is the very human element of seeking revenge or vengeance when you are either involved in such cases or know the people involved, or simply because you believe the offence is so wrong, so abhorrent, so repugnant to human nature that revenge must be a part of the punishment. These elements do exist. Let us not delude ourselves by saying they do not. With all members of the House, I believe it is necessary, in the kind of society in which we live, to provide opportunities for our families, friends and neighbours to walk the streets in safety and to protect our families and friends from crimes of violence which, unfortunately, have become so predominant.

I would point out that the dramas and other programs depicted on the television screen are bound to have some effect. I do not want to say things that perhaps ought not to be said, but it is not long ago that Senator Dodd of the United States headed a subcommittee of the Senate investigating the relationship between illustrations of crime on television and the growth of juvenile delinquency and crime. During the course of the inquiry a witness stated that one reason the growth of crime by juveniles had not spread was that many of these television shows were broadcast at a late hour and therefore were not seen by many young people. The television executives, after reading that evidence, immediately took steps to change the hour of these shows and brought them on earlier. I think this was a shocking thing to do. speechtext:
I beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker. I devoted a large part of my first speech on this topic to the history of capital punishment, hoping to make the point that there is nothing new in the principle of imposing the death penalty for capital crimes. The fact is that this principle has survived intact since the dawn of civilization. Let me say something to those who insist that we are more civilized now and that capital punishment is uncivilized. I invite them to suggest to me that those who commit the brutal and senseless crime of murder are entitled to all the benefits of our civilization. The coddling of a murderer in the name of humanity is not a civilized act. In my view, it is an irresponsible act.
I have said that some members must have been of two minds when they voted to give this bill second reading. I wonder if the government is hoping that the bill will be defeated in the coming vote. I do not know why they would take such a great risk if they really want to get this issue settled. If this is an election gimmick, I must say that the government is miscalculating badly. The consensus of all surveys I have seen on the subject weighs heavily in favour of capital punishment for capital crimes. The government must surely know by now that the Canadian people favour drastic measures to curb the rise in the rate of murder and other violent crimes.
When I spoke on this bill, I posed a hypothetical case for my colleagues and asked: If one of my colleagues was confronted in his home by an armed intruder and knew that he was about to be killed, would he shoot the intruder to save his own life? If the answer is yes, then there is the answer as to whether capital punishment is compatible with what we call civilized conduct. I cannot imagine anyone hesitating to kill a would-be murderer in defence of his own life. So why is there all the anguish and soul-searching about whether or not to take the life of a convicted murderer?
My sympathy is not with the armed intruder. My sympathy lies with the innocent victim of the intruder. My sympathy is with the law-abiding citizen who deserves the protection of those elected to represent him in parliament. We have a responsibility to protect innocent citizens against those who would take the law into their own hands, especially those who would take another life in the course of committing a heinous crime such as rape or kidnapping.
I cannot throw my support to a murderer simply because he is alive and the victim is dead. All too often the
Capital Punishment
victim is forgotten in the course of what is usually a long, hard-fought and expensive trial. All the instruments of justice are at the disposal of the murderer because he is still alive. None of the instruments of justice, none of the advantages of our great civilization is available to the victim because the victim is dead.
When this bill was first introduced in January, most of us here agreed that if capital punishment were to be retained for any crime, it should apply to the murder of a policeman or prison official killed in the line of duty. That provision was in the bill that we passed on second reading a few weeks ago, and it was part of the bill that was passed by parliament more than five years ago. It can be said, then, that this is indeed the will of parliament. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it was also the will of the parliament of 1967. We should now be debating the question of whether we will have capital punishment in Canada or whether it should be abolished. But we are not debating that at all. We debated a few weeks ago, and are again debating today, whether we should pass the buck to another parliament five years from now.
We are expected to make a decision. It has been shown by the present government that there is no point in delaying the decision for another five years. We have been told that over the next five years we will be able to accumulate valuable data that will help us to make a firm decision at some future date. That is what the government said in 1967. And what do we have? We have nothing, absolutely nothing in the way of valid data. This government has commuted every death sentence imposed by the courts of Canada for the crime of capital murder. All of us in the House know that this government imposed a total ban on capital punishment more than five years ago when it adopted the practice of commuting death sentences and, in so doing, made it impossible for us to determine whether the death penalty would indeed be a deterrent.
Today, a criminal who is determined not to get caught will not hesitate to shoot at a policeman. I recall the case of the Toronto policeman who was killed a few months ago when he stopped an automobile that was being driven erratically. The driver simply stepped out of his car and shot the policeman dead. A few days ago a policeman was shot three times in Peterborough when he went to investigate a suspected break-in at a supermarket. In these and other cases relating to the murder of policemen the penalty for the crime committed has been relatively minor. We find that policemen are becoming fair game for anyone who feels that murder is no more serious than break and enter or purse-snatching.
Surely it is the fault of parliament that so many people today lack proper respect for our laws and for our law enforcement officers. It is our fault that this situation has deteriorated to such an extent that a policeman can be shot dead while investigating a minor traffic infraction. We have to consider putting a higher price on the luxury of killing people. The earliest recorded laws of man provide for the execution of criminals for certain capital offences, it may well be that that is one of the reasons why civilization has been able to move forward. I feel certain in my own mind that if there had not been some provision in those early times for controlling the base impulses of man, these impulses would have been paramount and

Capital Punishment
would have won over the instincts that took man out of the caves and the trees.
There is already evidence in our country to show that the permissive policies of the present government are eating away at the fabric of our society and eroding the foundations of traditional concepts of law and order. The victims in this drama are the innocent, the law-abiding and those who want to preserve our society. The winners are those who scoff at our laws, sneer at our institutions and poison the minds of the young and the impressionable. They take all, and give nothing. In far too many cases they take the ultimate: they take another human life. I say again, Mr. Speaker, in far too many cases they take another human life bacause the price is too cheap. We have an extraordinary situation in existence today in this respect. We have a law in Ontario that provides for compensation for victims of violent crime. Almost daily someone is paid damages by the provincial government for injuries suffered by victims of shootings, muggings and other crimes. At the same time we are debating whether we should impose a penalty in kind on the person who inflicts the injury. There are scores of cases where victims of crime suffer the after effects for the rest of their lives, while the criminal serves a few months or a few years in jail and is then free to repeat the crime.
In the case of murder I cannot accept the premise that execution of a murderer does not bring the victim back to life or ease the burden on the victim's family, so there is no point in executions. There is a very valid point. The point is that murder should carry a price as high as the value of the life taken. Anyone who is prepared to take the life of another person, deliberately and calculatedly, should have to pay with his own life. To say that that is uncivilized is pure and utter rubbish. The life of a murderer is no more sacred that that of his victim. That, Mr. Speaker, is what we should be talking about here today.
I would like to answer those people who might construe my position as bloodthirsty. Nothing could be further from the truth. Anyone who draws that conclusion from my remarks has missed the point. The point is that we should be prepared to adopt the strongest possible measures against those in our society who do have a thirst for blood. We should be debating right now the issue of who in Canada is entitled to our protection. It is the law-abiding citizens and the victims of crime who are entitled to our sympathy and our support. I am tired of hearing about how important it is to spare the life of the murderer. In the name of civilization, let us recognize the true role of parliament in this matter. Let us establish once and for all that we do not place the life of the murderer on a higher plane than the life of the victim.
In concluding my remarks, I would like to say to my colleagues that the partial ban on capital punishment over the past five years has resulted in a totally unsatisfactory situation. As we know, it has really been total abolition. We have seen a gradual breakdown of law and order, and in respect for the law and law enforcement personnel.
In place of this bill I would rather have us impose capital punishment for all crimes of murder, where there are no extenuating circumstances, for a period of five

years. If this new law were followed to the letter, we would be able properly to assess the value of capital punishment as a deterrent. Another effect, I am sure, would be to place the value of life in the proper perspective. We would in time tend to place as high a value on the life of the victim as on the life of the murderer. This would bring a very worth-while result: if we were to do that, the majority of Canadians might come to feel that we in parliament have their true interests and their welfare at heart.

Mr. Speaker, I am entering this debate for the first time, although the subject was debated at some length before being sent to the committee. We are now on the report stage, considering amendments which in one way or another would modify the objectives set out in the bill. The bill as originally submitted by the government would continue the law as it existed from 1967 to 1972, imposing a ban on capital punishment except when murder was committed against police officials or penitentiary personnel.
In 1967 it was my opinion that we should give limited abolition a trial, to demonstrate the effect it might have in alleviating some of the concern felt by the public generally, while at the same time establishing a certain degree of protection for specific categories of people in our society who assume special responsibilities for us in the field of law enforcement. Unfortunately, in that five-year period the government ignored the legislation. Even in cases where capital murder was committed against police officials and penitentiary guards, action was not taken to impose the death penalty. As a result, the legislation was really a fraud, or a farce. Members of parliament were duped, because they had voted for something which never happened. Now, five years later, we are asked to extend the legislation for a further five years. What the government is asking us to do, in effect, is to support the complete abolition of capital punishment under the guise or the pretence that is would be implemented in the case of capital murder of police officials and penitentiary guards.
The amendment before us would extend the area in which capital murder calls for the death penalty. Specifically, it relates to rape in the course of which the victim is killed. Really, the amendment involves only one segment of the offence of capital murder. I believe it should cover all cases of capital murder where there is in the mind of the person committing the offence a deliberate intention

July 24, 1973
Capital Punishment
to carry out the action in question. There is some doubt in my mind as to this amendment because this type of murder often takes place in the absence of any deliberation. It is a crime of passion. It is a crime often committed by a person of unbalanced mind, a person who really requires special mental treatment. Perhaps such a person should be classified more often under the category of non-capital murder rather than murder. There are many such instances.
I cannot say I am a strong retentionist, because I believe that if the system worked properly abolition could be achieved. I cannot agree with one of the amendments proposed, to the effect that capital murder be completely abolished but that people be kept in penal institutions for 20 or 25 years. I believe the only way in which a rehabilitation program works in institutions is by the provision of some hope to inmates that if they are able to indicate they are rehabilitating themselves and are preparing themselves for return to society, society will give them an opportunity to return. But they must indicate that they have learned their lesson and can make a worth-while contribution for the remainder of their lives.
From that point of view I could not under any circumstances support any amendment to the effect that people be placed in penal institutions, much as people are placed in mental institutions, for the rest of their lives. I think there is nothing more inhumane than to say to a person that there is no hope left for him and that the rest of his life should be spent in a solitary way within an institution. From that point of view some arguments which have been offered have given me a great deal of concern.
At the same time, I believe society in general feels, because of the many things that have happened within our penal institutions, because of the increase of crime in the nation, because of the coddling of inmates in institutions, and because of a breakdown in the effectiveness of the rehabilitation programs that have been in effect in Canada or which supposedly are in effect, that parliament should restore, at least for a limited period, the death penalty because it lays a foundation on which a system can be built which says that at least the paid killers who roam the streets of our nation, if they commit this type of crime will pay with their lives.
If the government is desirous of securing the abolition of the death penalty-and I have no objection to that objective because I believe it is the ultimate objective in an enlightened society-it must first prove to the people of Canada that there is a system operating within our penal institutions which guarantees the ultimate security of the public. I believe there is a very strong feeling among the public generally that the death penalty should be retained because of the lack of confidence members of the public have in the type of penal rehabilitation programs in effect at the present time. While some people may say the two are not related-and perhaps they are not-I think in the main they are. I believe the public feel that because of the way we have been playing around with this subject it is not receiving the protection desired; therefore the public is urging members of parliament to give it the ultimate protection.

When parliament moves as strongly against the views of the public as was indicated on second reading, then I believe the public becomes very alarmed about parliament and the fact that parliament does not speak for it. If parliament does not speak for the public on this issue, then it is very easy for the public to conclude that parliament does not speak for it on any issue. I think this is one of the mistakes in respect of this debate and the whole concept adopted by the federal government.
I was very disappointed when the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) suggested he would propose the complete abolition of capital punishment by amendment of the original legislation. Then the public really became upset and said that the government did not care what the people of Canada thought. The public generally expressed concern that there was not a full return to retention of the death penalty, and the fact that the government had the unmitigated gall, through the Solicitor General, to suggest that parliament go further and completely do away with capital punishment rather than merely for another five years.
Cartoons sometimes display the views of people better than anything else. An interesting cartoon appeared on the editorial page of the Daily Colonist of Victoria, British Columbia, the other day. It depicted the Solicitor General pouting. There was this inscription:
Warren Allmand is my name,
Abolition is my game,
The death penalty is unfair,
As for murder victims, they're gone-why care?
Through the Commons it will be rammed.
Public opinion? Public opinion be damned.
That is the unfortunate history of this debate. This is a description of parliament because parliament does not mirror the views of the public and its apprehension about the state of affairs in this country, especially in so far as law enforcement and penal reform are concerned. At times I believe the Solicitor General could stand a sense of humour. Recently Harold Ballard received a ticket of leave. This type of leave from prison has been provided a great many times to people all across this country, some of whom have committed much more dastardly crimes.
I might say I do not know Mr. Ballard, I have never met him and I do not know any member of his family. I come from Nova Scotia, and he comes from Toronto. However, I can say that this man has a sense of humour, because having done all the things he has done at his age, it must have been a terrible thing for him to face the consequences of his acts and serve a term in a penal institution. He came out of the institution and made some humorous crack about the institution. Nobody in his right mind would have thought the man was serious when he was speaking about filet mignon being served, and this sort of thing. But what did the Solicitor General do? He was really uptight about this. He thought it was shocking and that the fellow should never be allowed out of the institution.
At the same time, in recent history this government is said to have had great compassion for Yves Geoffroy, a convicted killer. He killed his wife. They were so con-
July 24, 1973

cerned about that man that they let him out of prison so he could marry someone else and provide another mother for his children. To me the situation indicates the type of thinking and the inconsistency of this government as related to this debate. All Harold Ballard did was to admit he still had a sense of humour even though he was in a penal institution. What Yves Geoffroy did was commit an unthinkable act and none of us can have any respect for him. Mr. Geoffroy was even allowed to go for his honeymoon out of the country, whereas Mr. Ballard will not even be allowed out for weekends, even for good behaviour.
Some sense of proportion must be put back into the whole matter of capital punishment, penal reform and all the questions related to the subject before I can support the abolition of capital punishment. I say to this government: Prove to me, to members of parliament and to the people of this country that you have a sensible, realistic and reasonable program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to speak to the amendment of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) referred to as the Morin amendment, a term which I believe is out of order. The hon. member for Louis-Hebert has suggested attaching to section 214 of the Criminal Code two further categories of crime for which a convicted person would receive the death sentence-not only for the murder of police officers and prison guards but for death ensuing kidnapping, or death which takes place in the case of rape. So now, according to the amendment, we would expand to four exceptions what is generally the abolition of capital punishment as proposed by the government. This creates a conundrum that murder is murder, and why should the lives of certain people be more valuable than the lives of others?
I think we would have to look at this question in another light. If this bill is defeated, then not only would the person who commits murder while committing rape be liable to a charge of murder, and those who commit homicide when involved in a kidnapping be liable to a charge of murder, but it would widen the scope to the degree contained in section 213 of the Criminal Code which provides: Culpable homicide is murder where a person causes the death of a human being while committing or attempting to commit treason or an offence mentioned in section 52, piracy-
Which would involve hijacking.
-escape or rescue from prison or lawful custody-
Which would cover prison guards.
-resisting lawful arrest, rape-
Which would include the amendment of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert.
-indecent assault, forcible abduction-
Which includes kidnapping.
-robbery-
Which would cover the people who murder bank tellers and customers in banks.
-burglary or arson, whether or not the person means to cause death to any human being and whether or not he knows that death is likely to be caused to any human being-
So really the suggestion of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert that we increase the exception to the government's legislation so that offences punishable by death be not only the murder of prison guards and police officers, but also murder as a result of rape or kidnapping, would be adequately covered if the government's bill were defeated.
I do not believe that we should clutter our statute books with more exceptions. It appears that every day we make an exception to this and an exception to that, rather than painting the broad picture. Therefore, my tendency at this

July 24, 1973
Capital Punishment
time is to vote against the amendment, hoping that its proponents will not feel that I am voting against the idea. In fact, I hope that the mover of the amendment will vote against the government's bill, because in defeating it she will gain what she seeks.
Once more we are debating capital punishment, Mr. Speaker. Although I am in my freshman term, it is interesting to me that this parliament has its priorities reversed. For some years there was discussion on changing the family allowance legislation so that many law-abiding people who are contributing in a useful way to society would be better able to do so. Now we have decided to deal with capital punishment, with the government's legislation proposing more benefits for the criminal element and murderers. We are discussing this question instead of trying to help people in need of financial assistance through such means as a revised family allowance plan.
When this bill was first introduced it was introduced with priority over increasing old age pensions. It was introduced with priority over increasing the veterans allowance. It was introduced with priority over reducing income taxes. What I am concerned about is that the government has proposed to confer benefits on criminals with priority over conferring benefits on the law-abiding citizens of the country who foot the bill. I feel that this is improper.
In the month of June, in response to a question from me, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) indicated that at that stage there was no person in Canada who had committed culpable homicide, who had gone through his preliminary hearing, his trial and all appeal stages, including appeal to the Supreme Court, and was awaiting the death sentence. Indeed, I believe that is still the case. But although no person has exhausted all the legal remedies in connection with the killing of a police officer or prison guard, we are spending the time of this House discussing capital punishment. We could easily be discussing family allowance legislation to put more money into the pockets of law-abiding Canadians at an earlier stage than can now be expected simply because we are giving it lower priority than affording murderers extra benefits.
Dealing with this particular amendment-and as others come along I may wish to talk briefly about them-I feel we should not make further exceptions. I hope that the government's legislation will be defeated. If it is, then the Morin amendment-if I may call it so-will take effect because we will be returning to the Fulton formula of 1961 according to which a person, no matter what offence he committed, if he committed a murder in the process could be charged with murder or with the original offence. I say this with some background in criminal law; I prosecuted criminals for over three years in the capital of Canada. I discussed the matter at some length with the senior Crown attorney this morning, just to refresh my memory because I have not been active practising criminal law for a year. I wished to assure myself that this was the case. As I say, the hon. member for Lous-Hebert will succeed if the government's bill is defeated.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to miss the opportunity of giving ny opinion on this amendment.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, where the government wants to come to. Five years ago, we tenaciously pleaded to maintaining capital punishment in Canada and, in spite of all our efforts, the government succeeded in having a motion passed by the House to the effect that capital punishment would be abolished for a trial period of five years, whereas we had the evidence that 90 per cent of the population was against this legislation. The proposal was accepted and today, five years later, when the law made two exceptions for the murder of prison guards and policemen, such murders occurred and the law was not applied.
Today, we ask for a new extension of five years, and I would like to ignore the bomb the Sollicitor General (Mr. Allmand) launched in this House by saying that he wanted total abolition of capital punishment. I no longer understand anything. In fact I fail to understand the Liberals or the Progressive Conservatives and still less the members of the New Democratic party.
For the NDP, it is a total contradiction. There are in this party disappointing contradictions. They simply want to give death to the fruit of rape, and they are going to vote against the death penalty for rapeists. On one side, they will vote for abortion which is the fruit of rape and on the other side they are going to vote against an amendment asking for capital punishment for those who commit rape. Thus the situation in this House is incomprehensible; it seems to have become a Tower of Babel.
Once again, I wonder where the government wants to come to; does it want to extend indefinitely the study of the matter or is it trying by all means not to submit this question to the people's will. What we are pressing for is a referendum. We are here to serve the will of the people. Let us have a referendum and then we can pass legislation accordingly. But no! We are having lengthy discussions on whether capital punishment will be abolished as well as under what circumstances it should be abolished. I support the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) which says that capital punishment will be imposed, and I quote:
(b) in respect of a male person, where such person causes the death of a female person while committing or attempting to commit rape.
Attempting to commit rape. I want to come back to those words because the hon. member for Louis-Hebert corrected my colleague a while ago when she said that the amendment merely suggested that capital punishment should be imposed upon those who commit rape. But the amendment goes on to say, and I quote:
-or attempting to commit rape,
However, if the hon. member for Louis-Hebert reads the amendment carefully she will see that it says "attempting to commit rape." But here again this amendment is a monumental farce. I will be voting for that farce because I am for capital punishment in all cases of murder.
The hon. member for Louis-Hebert says-and I understand her feelings as she is a woman-that when a man
July 24, 1973

rapes a woman the death penalty should apply. Today there are men who are nearly carnivorous, and she foresees that. But do you know that there are also tigress women who can eat and rape men? Do you know also that there are homosexuals who eat men? In those cases too, let us have a general application of the act.
Homosexuality was legalized but here again even though rape is somewhat legalized today the issue is no longer raised. In the past, rape was punishable by death; today, it is a normal thing. However, I wish to call the attention of the House to a still more serious issue. The death penalty will be inflicted for rape, when we know that rapists are mentally unbalanced like homosexuals. They are sick and mentally unbalanced those who will be condemned to death.
It will readily be seen-and this is what I hate-that it is somewhat like setting up a cock-fight with lawyers. It is easy to imagine the lawyers in court; such a nice fight! Was it a rape or not? The witness is not there, she is dead. Now the rape will be discussed for a year or two and after it is ascertained, it will then be proved that the accused is mentally unbalanced. The death penalty will no longer be involved because it will have been proved that the accused is a sick person. That is why I suggest that the amendment is but a grain of sand, a monumental farce, for it is too incomplete and will lead to interminable discussions before the courts on the matter of rape.
In spite of it all, Mr. Speaker, I think I shall vote for the amendment. I heard some hon. members say they opposed the amendment because they favour restoring the death penalty. To my mind, that is fighting somewhat with opposites, because if you are in favour of the whole, you must also be in favour of the parts, however minimal. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the part is very minimal, but I shall still support it; and I hope the hon. member for Louis-Heb-ert understands that we are here to do the will of the people. If the people want such and such a regulation to be passed by referendum-the usual procedure-I hope Parliament will respect their wishes, especially in view of all the requests that were sent out, five years ago, to the Minister of Justice. I feel that should be sufficient to prevent once more these discussions that will drag on and will end up with a five year extension.
But, let us at least do the contrary: Let us reinstate capital punishment for five years. It has been removed for five years without success. Let us reinstate it for five years; we will see what happens. Let it be reinstated for five years, but, this time, the minister should cease to commute death penalties into 20, 15 or 7 years of imprisonment. There is no justice any longer. But who prostitutes justice? It is not the Canadian public, Mr. Speaker; it is those on the benches, the lawyers. That is why people do not believe anymore in justice, they consider it as a gigantic farce, and they are partly right.
However, Mr. Speaker, coming back to the amendment, I say that I shall vote for it and I sincerely hope that the reinstatement of the capital punishment will be passed for a five year period.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not availed myself of an opportunity to speak on this
Capital Punishment
measure, but I feel compelled to speak on the motion of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin). In the short time that the hon. member has been with us we have learned that she represents her constituents with a real sense of responsibility. There is no doubt in my mind that when she proposed this motion she had their welfare and the welfare of the majority of citizens of Canada at heart and had no desire for personal publicity.
I have no hesitation in supporting the principle of the motion because I think what the hon. lady is trying to do in this day and age is very sound. She is trying to bring in an amendment to enlarge the jurisdiction of Canada so that the death penalty will apply to cases of rape, attempted rape or kidnapping where murder is committed.
I will not burden the House with figures and with what has happened in the past in this country and in other countries, because that would not be pertinent to the measure with which we are dealing. We are entering into a brand new phase all over the world, and we must evolve new laws and new regulations for coping with the evolution through which we are going. The growing apathy and lack of responsibility shown by many in Canada as well as in other countries is causing many people great uneasiness and concern. We must be guided by something. Perhaps we shall need to control the emotions of those who cause harm to others by instilling a sense of fear or by showing force. We shall need to do that until we are thoroughly convinced that other ways of restraining people are just as effective.
Today there is not that assurance. Today the churches and schools do not influence the thinking and conduct of people as they did in the past. Certainly, our schools do not influence our philosophy of living as once they did. As well, the change in our way of living has brought a change in the influence of the family itself. At one time the family controlled its own members. All this change is happening at once. It is almost as if we are like a ship without a rudder. We are losing many of the guides that determined conduct in Canada in past years. Without those guides we sometimes flounder in our attempts to achieve something.
I do not think what we do in Canada should necessarily be the same as that done in other countries. For example, in the case of the Northwest Mounted Police, whose glorious hundredth anniversary we are celebrating this year, Canada departed from normal practice and established this first-class police force. With it we proved that a few responsible individuals are able to maintain order and peace if they are backed by the authority of government. Hon. members will recall that then we sanctioned capital punishment. At that time passions were perhaps stronger than they are today, and crime went undetected sometimes for months.
I want to deal with the rape aspect of the hon. member's amendment and say why I think it is so necessary to consider imposing capital punishment. We are living in a new age. The young girls and ladies of our nation are without the protection of home and relatives that they had in previous years. Our womenfolk are going out into the world, into the labour force and entering all aspects of Canadian life which are changing. We have industrial
5932

July 24, 1973
Capital Punishment
areas such as we never had before. We live in concentrated areas, packed elbow to elbow as never before. Such conditions create tensions and chaotic situations such as we have never before experienced and did not anticipate.
Many crimes take place because our way of living has changed, because many people are concentrated in small areas. We eat differently, live differently and work differently, and our churches and schools do not exert the same influence on us. The family is different too. That is why the crime rate is going up as it has never gone up before. Under these conditions we must take further measures in order to safeguard our people.
Let me deal with the other aspect of the hon. lady's motion, kidnapping. I was interested in the minister's remarks of Monday last. He almost sloughed off the suggestion that we should impose capital punishment for kidnapping ensuing in death and said that where a murder is committed in connection with kidnapping, the murder perhaps was not contemplated. Mr. Speaker, murder is murder, and it is only one man's opinion against another as to whether murder was contemplated or not.
As society becomes more complicated and more affluent, and tremendous sums of money become involved in our dealings, the temptation for kidnapping is greater than ever in history. Many countries worry about the safety of their ambassadors and respresentatives living in other countries. These people are being kidnapped and held for ramson, sometimes with disastrous results. In air piracy, entire groups of people are exposed to what may be contemplated murder.
In considering the phase into which we are now entering, and the new lifestyle which is now emerging in Canada as well as in other countries, it behooves us as representatives of the people to look at these questions in a manner different from that of five years ago. It is no use the government saying that there is no proof that capital punishment will restrain any of these violent crimes since, equally, there is no proof that it will not. Should we, as representatives of the people who are concerned about the safety of the nation, gamble and say that perhaps capital punishment will not act as a deterrent; or should we assume our responsibilities of safeguarding the majority of Canadians against the violence of the majority, and not gamble? This is what we must consider seriously.
In some quarters one hears tremendous expressions of sympathy for a minority of people involved in these crimes. It is said, perhaps on compassionate grounds, that what was done was not contemplated, that it was an accident or the result of undue influence of drugs, intoxicants or something like that. For how long can we make excuses for those who commit these crimes and show such callous disregard for their victims and the families of their victims? I do not think we are justified in adopting that attitude. That is why I have no difficulty in supporting the amendment of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert.
The hon. lady's amendment amply reflects the majority feeling of the people I have the honour to represent. The people of my riding-as of the hon. lady's, I am sure-are most concerned about what is going to happen in Canada. Fifteen years ago we did not think that women would be afraid to walk the streets of our cities at night. We did not think that police would patrol in pairs for reasons of

additional safety. We knew what was happening in other countries; we did not think it could happen in Canada. I wonder if the softening of our laws has perhaps not contributed to some of the conditions we face today. Some say that the crime rate in Canada is not increasing more quickly than anywhere else. Certainly, once our society became more permissible, conditions were ripe for the violence that existed in other countries to be introduced into Canada.
I am very pleased to have had an opportunity to speak on this subject today and lend my support, on behalf of the people I represent, to the hon. lady. She is to be complimented for the fact that in her first session in this House, and on a subject as deep, complicated and as important as this, she has taken the time and trouble to research the subject and to assess the feelings of those she has the honour to represent. As a woman and a mother, she has brought this amendment to parliament. I have the greatest admiration for her and I ask the House to support this amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like in turn to make a few comments on the amendment now before the House.
Like many members, I have participated in the debate on second reading and I find the amendments under consideration very thoughtful. I agree with the remarks of the previous speaker and with the congratulations that he has offered to the representative from Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin), in view of the value of the said amendment as well as its necessity in the present context.
According to the amendment now before the House, capital punishment would apply in cases of kidnapping or rape following which the victim is murdered. Now, it is important to recognize the merits of this amendment in view of the problems which multiply every year and that we experience in our life. According to me, the fact of presenting this amendment at this stage is justified and altogether timely if the problems facing our society because of this are to be seriously acknowledged.
Of course, the member who spoke before dealt with the major changes which happened in our society and showed that our traditions and certain principles are unfortunately fading away, and that the influences certain sectors had on the good behaviour of citizens have also diminished, if not disappeared. That is why then I think that it is more and more becoming that this amendment be adopted and, according to me, if we had a real national enquiry 95 per cent of the people would be for this amendment.
I think quite honestly that 95 per cent of the people welcome this amendment which perfectly satisfies the needs for security which they are entitled to.
This amendment is important, most significant and very well presented. I too take this opportunity to congratulate the sponsor of the motion. I also wonder how this amendment can be implemented, in the light of the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In fact, he said quite clearly that as Prime Minister he would certainly not be in favour of the death penalty.

We know perfectly well that in our present system, it is up to the Cabinet to allow or disallow the application of the death penalty. I therefore feel that it would be very important for all hon. members to demand that the Prime Minister agree to respect the decision and the will of this House. If you look at the statistics of the past five years, you will see quite clearly that Parliament had decided to suspend capital punishment, except in two instances, the murder of a policeman or a prison guard.
We know perfectly well that this decision made by Parliament has not been respected. In fact, we are now presented with this legislation aimed at continuing this experiment for another five years, and at considering the possibility of maintaining the death penalty for two categories of murder, namely the murder of police officers and prison guards. The amendment now before us provides for the death penalty in two more cases, rape and kidnapping where the victim is murdered, but we are never given any assurance that the Prime Minister will respect either this amendment or the decision that will be made.
If this amendment gathers the support of the majority of the hon. members-and I hope that it will-in view of the Prime Minister's statement, we will have to question ourselves seriously, we will have to believe that we are speaking in the wind, unless the hon. member who introduced the motion can obtain from the government the assurance that it will respect the decision of the majority of the members. I think that people expect the government to respect any decision taken by Parliament on such an important matter, which is one of those rare occasions when a free vote is held. And the majority of the hon. members have proved that this is so; they are expressing themselves freely.
Thus, it is imperative that the Prime Minister, in this debate, should commit himself in a very particular way to respect the decision taken by Parliament. Then, we shall have good reason to believe that the amendment will be followed through, which I hope.
Of course, at the second reading stage, I brought up many times, in my speech, the importance of establishing prevention procedures. The Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) can talk of rehabilitation.
Much has been done in the last few years about rehabilitation. I think it would be more important to try to establish prevention procedures in our society.
I am doubtful in my mind about rehabilitation at 40, 50 or 60. But where the government has much work to do, for the prevention of cases such as those mentioned in the amendment, is in the development of prevention procedures. To identify dangerous environments which effectively are responsible for young men going wrong.
I believe that capital punishment is not a solution per se, but considering that we do not seem to have more valid solutions, I believe that a person which has taken upon itself to take the life of a citizen deserves no less than death. Kidnapping or rape followed by murder is a very serious offence which has been more and more current these last few years. So, considering the fundamental changes in our society, it is interesting to note that the
Capital Punishment
hon. member for Louis-Hebert has moved this amendment which is the perfect answer to present-day needs.
I hope most hon. members will support this amendment which meets present needs. Indeed, there was no need for it 15 or 20 years ago, but every day we witness some unfortunate incidents which makes it necessary to implement such a measure.
I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that the few comments I made on this amendment will receive the support of a majority and, above all, that the Prime Minister will undertake to comply with the decision made by most members of this House. Then, we shall have done a good job.

speechtext:
It is over two months ago that I rose in the House to speak in the debate on capital punishment. Now I find myself on my feet again. I should like to reflect on one or two remarks I made in May which I think have some validity today. I said the question of imposing the death penalty was one of the problems which plague our society. I said the government had brought down stop-gap legislation to be dealt with at a time when we should be addressing ourselves to economic issues of real importance. I said the Criminal Code already contained provisions adequate to deal with this subject, so the legislation need not be brought in at this time.
I said, further, that it was a bad bill, so confusing that the abolitionists would support it even though it provided for capital punishment. In my view, the bill gave the abolitionists no real choice when it came to voting. It was typical of the government to have behaved in this way. If they had felt this was an important issue, they could have called parliament together in November or December to deal with it. In fact, the official opposition urged the government to do just that. Nevertheless, here we are today concerning ourselves, at this point, with an amendment moved by the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin).
A great deal has been said since I made my own contribution to the debate earlier this year. I am still in favour of capital punishment; more so, if anything, having heard the speeches made from the other side of the House. I favour capital punishment. For this reason I find myself in agreement with the amendment. At least it is a step in the right direction. If I had a choice, I would go further than the amendment does, but we have to start somewhere.
It is curious, but if this amendment is passed it might deter someone from voting in favour of the bill as amended, for the reason that the bill calls for capital punishment for the murder of police officers and prison guards, and someone who agreed with that might take the view that a rapist was a sick person and should not be sentenced to death. This is a further indication of the fact that one law is needed for everybody. We do not want various degrees of capital punishment-I guess there is only one degree of capital punishment. There is capital murder, which is described adequately in the law, and therefore we should have capital punishment which would then fit the crime: There is no suggestion we should hang or otherwise execute someone who had committed a murder on compas-
5934

July 24, 1973
Capital Punishment
sionate grounds. It is wrong to have two categories of murder, one allowing a special status to prison guards and police.
If murderers are to be sentenced to life imprisonment, it is true there is no further penalty, which would deter them from escaping by whatever means possible, including murder. The worst that could happen to them would be to return to serve a further life sentence. If the law were less confused, its administration would be less confused and the government of the day would not be faced with the difficult task of deciding whether to commute death sentences or not. We have heard about the dilemma confronting juries which may feel clemency is deserved in certain cases. But again, if there were a rigid set of rules, juries would not be faced with this problem.
We are living today in a complex society, one in which it is impossible that each individual should receive the attention he might wish to receive or which he may think he deserves. In these circumstances, rigid rules are needed so that people may know where they stand. I am amazed at the arguments put forward by the abolitionists. They say it is the fault of society that murders are committed, and that murderers should not be put to death. I counter this assertion by saying that in today's complex society, if a man cannot cope with the situation I do not think there is any way in which the do-gooders will be able to correct him after he has committed a murder.
They say killing is wrong. Well, it is only wrong some of the time. They condone killing in the course of a war. Also, I am sure, they would not submit to a personal attack without reacting. And perhaps murder would be the result of that. They also say capital punishment has no deterrent value. I suggest that capital punishment is a deterrent, as are other penalties. We are brought up from earliest childhood to know there are penalties attached to certain acts, whether a spanking on mother's knee or a slap with a ruler in the classroom or, later on, a fine for some breach of the law, or a jail sentence and, finally, the death penalty. People are educated to understand that acts which are abominable to society are subject to penalties.
Statistics cannot prove that capital punishment has no deterrent value because, of course, the crimes which are prevented do not form part of the statistics. I find it curious that the abolitionists should feel they must pay more attention to a very small group of murderers who are probably not worthy of their consideration, while forgetting the millions of old people who built this country and who are suffering a worse fate, probably, than imprisonment. We have heard about the state of our prisons these days. They have been likened in the press recently to motels and nice vacation resorts.
We have heard many arguments put forward on religious grounds but there is no clear consensus emerging from them. There are clergymen in this House whose opinions differ on this question, and anyone who wishes to quote scripture can certainly find a text which will suit whatever argument he wishes to present.
