speakeroldname: Mr. Mark Rose (Fraser Valley West) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW BOARD
speechtext:
that Bill C-36, to establish an administrative review board, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to see the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) leave the chamber. I know he will be around for the debate tomorrow on the Olympic bill, but I have something to say which perhaps compared to any other business will be more meaningful to this particular minister than any other.
My initiation of this debate today through the means of private members' public bill C-36 comes, I hope, under the heading of a positive suggestion designed to ameliorate certain problems I have encountered since becoming a member of this House. It could be argued, I suppose, that the matter with which I propose to deal could have been handled better under a resolution rather than a private bill. But whatever the means, I believe it to be important to make the point here that a problem exists, and with an ever-growing public service this House should begin to
July 24, 1973

concern itself with a solution which may not be possible through some other measure.
For the benefit of those members wishing to speak in this debate, I will summarize the problem and my suggestions for a solution before I go into any great detail. Let us take the case of a public servant who has a problem, who has been denied a promotion, who has been allegedly unfairly discplined or who has been refused a transfer to some other area of the country. This public servant, after exhausting the normal avenues of appeal or grievance through the Public Service Staff Relations Act, comes ultimately to his MP seeking justice. Usually, the MP has little alternative but to write the minister seeking a review of the case on behalf of the public servant. The minister sets the wheels in motion. Perhaps he has time to do little else. The case ultimately filters down to the public servant's superior who made the controversial decision in the first place.
I am sure many members have had this experience. Hence the problem. How much of an independent appeal or disinterested review of this man's case can be expected when the person in charge of the review is the identical person who made the original decision which is being questioned by the public employee through his MP? This is why as a proposal to get around this problem and to achieve a better method of dealing with grievances, I have suggested the establishment of an independent administrative review board.
Today, then, I would like to make a positive suggestion by calling for the establishment of an administrative review board to provide protection for our federal employees. Like many MPs, I have constituents who are federal employees and sometimes, because their problems are so desperate, they have written to me for assistance. Having made many representations on their behalf, I have begun to appreciate why they express such bitter exasperation.
I recall a specific case of a couple of years ago. A constituent whom we will call Mr. Jones had accepted a position in the Northwest Territories. Although he had accepted a position in the Northwest Territories, he still wanted to keep in touch with British Columbia. Most people who visit British Columbia feel the same way. However, the department could not accommodate his preferences. So because of other latent dissatisfaction, Mr. Jones applied for a transfer to northern British Columbia.
This request was denied by the director in Edmonton. Subsequently Mr. Jones applied for a transfer from the region. When this was turned down on the basis of there not being any vacancies, Mr. Jones appealed to me. I, in turn, appealed to the minister-in this case the then minister of national health and welfare-who generously agreed to review the case. The minister's reply was the same as the director's. It is no wonder. The minister passes the request on to his staff, who in turn pass it on to the deputy minister, who passes it on to the assistant deputy minister, who passes it on to his assistant, who passes it all the way down the line to the director in Edmonton, who prepares a reply for the minister, which eventually is passed on to me, and in turn to the constituent.
The trouble is that the director in Edmonton who prepares the reply for the minister is the same director who
Public Service
makes the decision in the first place. How can one expect anything else? A dispute such as this is a matter of interpretation. It is necessary to allow other interpretations to be heard by an impartial judge or board. Otherwise we have a situation of the proverbial sheriff who is also judge, jury and-if you will forgive me-executioner. Under the present system, how are the Mr. Jones's to get a fair hearing? I have a case involving a lady who worked in the UIC office. She wrote me and said:
If there were promotions the young got them without competition. The older had to apply and in most cases were told they didn't have the qualifications even in some cases for their own jobs. Even the casual young got preference over permanent older employees. They have tried to put in grievances through the union but the union rep. are employees and are working for promotion, so side with management.
I think that is natural enough. We all remember the celebrated case of Ann Booth. Miss Booth was striving to be a Liberal candidate and was dismissed by the CRTC. Her case was heard by the committee on broadcasting. I believe it was a unique case so far as civil servants are concerned. The broadcasting committee had power to recommend. Although the committee did make a recommendation, Miss Booth was unable to regain her position after she had been dismissed on the ground of political activity.
It is cases like those I have described which caused me to reflect on the present grievance procedure within the public service. As an example of the administrative inquiry, the grievance procedure itself tends to allow management to confirm their original decision. There is a tendency for people to want to save face and to back up their colleagues. I do not blame the individuals. It is quite natural for people to want to defend themselves. We all do it. This is not something involving merely civil servants or politicians. The point we must consider, however, is whether this allows for the fairest and most just appeal. And I would argue that this is not the present case.
I would suggest that an alternative to the present structure would be one similar to that of the Pension Review Board of the Department of Veterans Affairs. This board was introduced after considerable and persistent pressure had been applied by the veterans' organizations. The veterans' organizations argued that a new appellant procedure was necessary, one that would add a Pension Review Board that was independent of the department. Both the veterans' associations and the department are pleased with the new board. They have found that it has reduced much of the animosity that was felt previously in the department and directed toward the department. They suggest a number of reasons this is so. Today, I think one of the reasons, the most important reason, for separation is that separation itself allows a guarantee of protection for the case. But the veterans have found, as well, that within the new structure there is less pressure on the lower levels of the grievance procedure to want to be tight-fisted when it comes to handling the grievances of the veterans. So the net consequence has been liberalization-if you will pardon the expression-all along the line.
If we compare the new veterans' structure with the present public service grievance structure, we find that

July 24, 1973
Public Service
there is an outstanding difference. The present grievance structure is limited by section 91 of the act which provides:
-having completed the three levels of grievance, the adjudication is limited to cases of interpretation or application in respect of the employee, of a provision or a collective agreement or an arbitral award or the disciplinary action resulting in discharge, or suspension or financial penalty.
Of course, this leaves a great number of areas of grievance outside the bounds of the adjudication process. I submit that a review board would provide greater latitude to hear such grievances. But a call for fairness or justice is not just a moral question; it is not solely confined to a moral question. I think this is a very important point. It is also a matter of good organization. How badly has the morale of our public service been worsened because public servants do not have confidence in their grievance procedure? I submit, also, that they do not have confidence or the feeling that their rights are protected at present.
We note similar discontent among railroad workers. At present railroads have a court mechanism to hear grievances, but this court is staffed by the employer and it is responsible to the employer alone. Therefore, in effect it acts as a kind of kangaroo court. Decisions are known to have been made by this body that would never have stood up in a proper court, but it was all right for the kangaroo court. These decisions have resulted in disciplinary action-I have a sheaf of them-or brownie points, as they call them on the railroad, and in some cases even in dismissal.
Some might say that such a kangaroo court can be eliminated, depending on the bargaining power of the unions. However, the old-line parties have never exhibited an interest in rectifying the situation. Indeed, some have argued that the managements of railroads know that they can be a stubborn bargainer because the old-line parties will always send the men back to work if they dare to strike. They might be on the brink of such a situation at present. If that is the case, then we must be able to find some other means by which employees can express their grievances to management. In my opinion, a review board that is independent of the present administration in the civil service or even in the rail companies could allow for a more fair and more impartial hearing of grievances. Accordingly, the decisions that it would make would be treated with more respect and confidence by the men if the board and its members were truly independent of the government and of management.
This bill, then, is in response to the many frustrated individuals who have made representations to me, and I sympathize with them deeply. I have even to some extent sympathized with the ministers of the Crown because I realize that it is not ill-will that sends the representation to the person who makes the decision, then back through the minister to me and brings back the same answer that was given in the first place. I know it is not ill-will on the part of the ministers but, rather, it is a question of organization. The present administrative organization does not allow for the kind of independent review board that would be satisfactory to both parties. Usually it is only satisfactory to one party, and that is what is wrong.
If one were to examine the many individual cases, one would find that the majority of these grievances are due to

the fact that the federal government is, in a sense, a far-flung empire. We have people dispersed all over Canada, and therefore there exist many intermediaries between the individual with his problem and the minister in Ottawa. Of course, that leaves a lot of room for many personal problems and for tension, and that is what we have. Tension, if it is allowed to continue at a high rate, is bound to affect morale. It means, of course, that the minister must rely on his staff to provide the answers. Unfortunately, his staff is often the same staff that made the decision in the first place.
Common sense tells us that the most effective way of ensuring a fair examination of any case is to appoint someone different, someone other than the person who made the decision, to consider it in the second instance. What we must come up with is an effective substitute for physical proximity because our public service is dispersed. I hope that this review board will be part of that mechanism and will act to bring the two parties closer together.
To conclude, may I say that I know someone from the other side, and perhaps also from this side, will make the observation that the independent review boards under the Canada Pension Plan and considering veterans' cases are client-oriented and there is quite a different relationship between client and government agency and employee and government agency. I think it is a fair to say that to extend this principle of an independent review board- even though the two situations in the examples I have given are not congruent-is a worthy one. So it is worth while to consider that the principle of independence in terms of grievances is a valid one. Someone will say also that it should be done by the unions. I do not think the unions have that power within the present Public Service Staff Relations Act in their grievance procedure, and there are other impediments in the way.
In conclusion, I should like to say that in my view the federal government must set a good example for an effective employer-employee relationship and I believe that the place to start this is within the public service.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it particularly expedient that the bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) should come up for debate at this time. Anybody who helps to unravel and to make more digestible the mass of regulations, directives, rites, orders, controls and massive red tape which thwart and frustrate the contribution and working practices of hundreds of thousands of civil servants would be welcome, provided that such a board did not in itself constitute a further hazard to dealing expeditiously with the thousands of complaints and inequities which exist within the public service at present.
There are approximately 250,000 persons in the public service of Canada, and I am sure many of them feel they have justifiable grievances which they are hesitant to air through established procedures. An administrative review board, an independent body, might provide the outlet they seek. I have mentioned that there are some 250,000 persons in the public service of Canada. Of these, 63,000 are women. The federal government is the largest employer of women in the country. But the Archibald report on sex
July 24, 1973

and the public service found that 83 per cent of these women were concentrated in administrative support roles.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW BOARD
speechtext: This is where they belong.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW BOARD
speechtext:
This concentration does not reflect the levels of education or the competence of Canadian women. It was reported earlier this year that only 25 women in the public service earn more than $26,000. Another report I have shows that of these public servants earning $20,000 or more, 97.3 per cent are men while only 2.7 per cent are women. Whichever way it is viewed, the status of women in the upper echelons of the public service is admittedly bleak. I mention these figures to stress a matter which was raised in this House yesterday.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) was questioned about the abhorrent practice of rug-ranking which exists among women employees in the public service. This practice, which has existed throughout all of the five years in which the hon. member for Westmount has held that portfolio, is one to which the government has devoted minimal, if any, attention. This discriminatory practice was forcibly brought to the attention of the President of the Treasury Board in a recent brief submitted by the Association of the Public Service Secretaries. It had to be pointed out to the minister that rug-ranking is a system by which a secretary's job level is determined by the importance and rank of her boss rather than by her own abilities.
The brief recommended the immediate adoption of a point-rating system and an honest appraisal of the secretary's value and potential in working as part of the management team rather than as a chattel. The President of the Treasury Board, regrettably, had not read the brief of the Association of the Public Service Secretaries. When it was explained to him, he reacted with sympathy, so it is said, but with very little in the way of recommendations. In his reply yesterday he said that if members can suggest ways in which the situation can be corrected, he would be glad to consider them. He said he tought that the problem appeared to lie with the inability adequately to rank secretaries according to their competence. I do not think that approach, or that reply, is adequate to meet the situation which exists among women in the public service today. I think that a much more positive and practical approach on the part of the government would commend itself not only to women in the public service but to women in the country generally.
The report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women forcibly pointed out the basic difference between equality of rights and equality of opportunities for women. In speaking to this bill submitted by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), I contend that if an administrative review board could have the effect of helping to correct the inequities to which women in the public service have been subjected for years, it would be a worth-while measure.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Public Service
Rose) when he says that a board should be created not only to look out for abuses, but also to supervise federal government agencies. Here is the purpose of Bill C-36:
It is the function and duty of the Board to investigate and review any decision or recommendation made relating to a matter of administration and affecting any person or body of persons in or by any department or agency, or by any officer or employee thereof in the exercise of any power or function conferred on him.
Mr. Speaker, to my mind the bill is excellent from the administrative point of view. I should like to mention just one example to prove it. In the Canadian civil service, we need competent people, with a good command of both official languages, in order to provide services to the public. I know very well that there is a shortage of personnel in some federal departments.
Not long ago, a physician from Hull phoned me to ask if there was a job opening for his son-in-law. He is a young university graduate of 29, fully bilingual. He made an application and received an application form to fill from the Public Service Commission of Canada; he wrote an examination whose results were excellent: he got a 83% mark. But he was told on the phone by a Public Service officer: "If you had some political backing there would be some chances for you to get that job".
This has just happened, only 15 days ago. Mr. Speaker, I do not accept this procedure in the Public Service. They should take into consideration the skills of the candidate, not his political affiliation. Whatever he may be liberal, socred, new democrat or conservative, everyone has the right to earn a living in Canada and if after passing a serious examination there is a department which needs his services, he should not be told that he would need some assistance from a minister or some political organiser to be immediately hired to fill the position for which he made an application.
Mr. Speaker, this is terrible. And the guy gave me the name of the person who suggested to him on the phone that he find someone to obtain this position through political influence. Can you imagine that? If this is not settled I will disclose in the House the names of the people involved and I will show them what stuff I am made of.
Patronage dispenses do exist in the public service but there are even more of them among politicians and organizers. That a liberal, a new democrat, a conservative or a socred should recommend someone to help him get a job, I have no objection provided his application is treated fairly. They should take into account competence and bilingualism within the services-and God knows that we are short of bilingual and competent people able to speak both official languages fluently-because there still exist departments where we are dealt with in English. I do not want those people to be fired or told they are going to be replaced immediately but we need bilingual personnel in many departments. I will give the example of a federal organization, of a Parliamentary organisation: the Treasury Board. I am not referring to the Quebec, Ontario or Nova-Scotia Treasury but to the federal Treasury Board which should be controlled by a review board such as that mentioned in Bill C-36.

July 24, 1973
Public Service
We need bilingual secretaries but we are told by the Treasury Board that they are short of money. Therefore we cannot get any secretaries. The other day, I was reading a list of people made available to political parties. I noticed that four press attaches were made available to the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and that some were paid up to $25,000. per year. As for me I have been requesting one for three years and did not get even one. I do not know whether the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Lewis) has one but I know that the leader of the official opposition has four. We are told by the Treasury Board that they have no money.
It is that same Treasury Board which decides to spend thousands of dollars to have beautiful wall-to-wall carpeting and special tapestries fitted in ministers' offices. They are throwing money out of the windows because they are in power. And those from other parties who need help are set aside and are denied secretaries and press attaches under the pretence that we are a small group in the Commons, as if we had no right to be treated on the same footing as any other political party.
If there were not a board of patronage dispensers but an independent board as proposed under Bill C-36 to contend with abuses, to pintpoint them, to inform the people on the ways money is spent in Ottawa, we would probably be better served by the Treasury Board. It is a federal agency. I will be told that it is a matter of internal administration, but nevertheless it is a federal agency. An internal administration to offer everything to big parties and nothing to the other ones, I am fed up with that, Mr. Speaker, and no matter who sits on that internal administration board it is all the same to me, but I say that there are abuses and that we are not treated fairly. There you are!
If a board could tell the Treasury Board: Listen, take it easy with the rugs, they are almost six-inches thick and you practically need snowshoes to walk on them, I would agree, Mr. Speaker, you should come and have a look at the sort of rugs we have in our offices. I think that they are ten year old hand-me-downs from the ministers' offices, it took me six years to get air conditioning in my office on the sixth floor of the Centre Block, six years to get a small unit that doesn't even work that well. It is better than what I had, which was nothing, but it isn't very effective. It must have cost about $150 or $160. It took me six years to get that. The Treasury Board didn't have any money before that, it was "broke".
Now, I am asking for assistance, because my office is overloaded with work, and I'm told: We do not have the necessary money to give you a larger parliamentary secretariat. Mind you, what I am asking for is not a secretariat for my own riding, but one to deal with all the correspondence we receive from all parts of Canada. We do not even have the means to answer all the letters received, because the Treasury Board says: We have no money.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-36 provides for the setting up of a board composed of five members, independent of any political party, and not one which would take charge of the publicity or the propaganda for the party in power, or the official opposition party, the New Democratic Party or the Social Credit Party of Canada. It would be a board made up of independent members who would watch over

expenditures in Ottawa. Then you would see a change, considerable savings, and fairer treatment. You would no longer hear what I said in my opening remarks: If you had a little help from the bosses, a bit of political "pull", you would get the job you want, for which you applied.
Mr. Speaker, I said before that I would give names. I shall not give them today, but the House may rest assured that I will do so because I will not put up with a bureaucrat saying: "Go and see the political bosses and you stand a very good chance of getting the job"; when you are told bluntly: "We need you but we cannot hire anybody until we get the okay from a member of the party in power." This is what is going on at the present time.
If Bill C-36 could only open up the eyes and ears of those who are responsible for hiring, it would serve a useful purpose. If Bill C-36 only allowed the hon. member who introduced it to express his views and allowed me to express mine about the absurdities that occur not only in Ottawa but throughout the country it will have been most useful. We are told the same thing in Quebec, as far as the federal government is concerned and in western Canada: "You did not accept the party in power and you will be punished for that."
Mr. Speaker, I think that the time for punishment is over. We need justice. We must treat people as human beings, regardless of their political affiliation. It is normal to speak about elections during the electoral campaign, but once it is over, it is very bad to reward one at the expense of the other, or not to take ability into account. I think this has lasted only too long. That sort of thing took place 40, 30, 25 years ago but in 1973 it is outmoded. Then we should get back in fashion. Let us bring in the fashion of dealing with Canadians; let us treat them as Canadians and not as supporters of political parties, which is something I deeply regret right now.
As for Bill C-36, I know that it will not pass. It will not be voted on. The parliamentary secretary to the minister is prepared to rise in order to talk it out. Another member will rise to speak. We will not vote on that bill, but yet it has its significance, if they wish to put some order in the federal administration, since there is none right now. We must provide for more justice in the administration; we must administer in view of the country and not the party.
[ English]

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the pleasures of a member of this House of Commons is to listen to the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette). However, I would say that it is not really a pleasure to have to follow him after he has just made a speech in this House. He has a command of language and imagery, although I would not want to confuse that with having a command of logic and necessary facts. While he was speaking he did, almost by accident, it seems to me, touch upon some of the things covered by the bill.
Perhaps I might reply to him and answer a number of questions that he raised outside the scope of the bill but which I believe to be rather important not only to him but to all other members. They deal basically with the provi-
July 24, 1973

sion of staff for members of parliament and particularly for the leaders of the parties.
Hon. members may not be aware that for some time now I have tried to place on the order paper a question designed to find out exactly the staffing provided by the House of Commons for the leaders of the various political parties. That was not possible because that information comes through the Speaker of the House. However, I want to tell the hon. member through you, Mr. Speaker, that I did obtain that information. It is available and I will undertake to have it delivered to his office tomorrow so that he can be aware of exactly what staffing is provided through the House of Commons to members of parliament and particularly to all party leaders. He will be able to discover the formula that is used for the allocation of the moneys of the House of Commons to provide him with his staff.
Concerning his office furniture, rugs, and whatnot, I am happy to tell him that he is not being furnished with cast-offs from ministers but that it is all new. He does not need to worry about being given what ministers no longer want. I hope the hon. member will understand that there is a distinction to be drawn between the administration of the civil service and the House of Commons; it is not a case of Treasury Board being niggardly in the provision of services to members of parliament but, rather, of our making a judgment as to how much we require and how this amount is to be divided between ourselves.
I should like to turn to the subject matter of this bill. Until the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) agreed to bring it forward last Friday, I had not had an opportunity to look at it. I wanted to find out what the government thought of this bill and whether or not it should be proceeded with. Unfortunately, there was some difficulty in determining the precise nature of the bill and there was confusion over a number of the phrases contained in the bill.
I will not go into detail except to say that it was felt that the drafting was not adequate. There was confusion as to whether the hon. member was trying to deal solely with the grievances of public servants which arise from time to time or, perhaps, more importantly, with the grievances which citizens being served by public servants might have. Apparently we would be dealing with two different aspects. However, the wording of the operative clauses was such that it was not clear to the officials who examined the bill or to myself which route we ought to take.
Unfortunately, today I am in the embarrassing position of having prepared some remarks on the ombudsman aspect which applies to citizens and not on the aspect to which my hon. friend addressed himself, which is specifically how we deal adequately with the grievances of public servants who feel that they have not obtained a square deal from their immediate supervisor.
I will be the first to deny that this is not an important subject and not an important area of concern for many public servants. Like the hon. member, I have had occasion to take up the cause of public servants who feel they have been wronged and not treated properly by a supervisor. Unfortunately, members of parliament often have not
Public Service
been able to act because there is a union organization in the field which is responsible for considering these grievances, taking them up with the government and arriving at adequate solutions. These organizations are new in many areas, particularly in areas such as the one I represent, which consists of a considerable area of northern Ontario. These unions have not been able to set up a properly functioning operation in order to process the grievances of public servants in such areas. I have taken up a number of cases but have not been able to obtain complete satisfaction. I have not satisfied myself or the public servants involved, because we have always had to reckon with the interposition of the union between the public servant concerned and the government.
Whether we think they are efficient or not, we must recognize that unions are responsible for considering grievances brought forward by their members, and they must deal adequately with those by approaching the Public Service Commission or Treasury Board, as the case may be.
The bill brought forward by the hon. member indicates that he feels, as do other members, that some other method must be discovered for dealing with these matters. At the moment he obviously feels that the present method is not satisfactory, and I tend to agree with him. My solution would not be one which he proposes, namely, the setting up of an independent administrative tribunal, but, rather, one which encourages, perhaps even forces if necessary, the union involved to take up the cudgels on behalf of its members.
I recognize the dilemma involved in setting up a properly effective and operative union organization in this way, give the nature of our country and the difficulties inherent in screening properly the quality and quantity of complaints brought forward for attention. Without doubt the problem is genuine. However, it is my feeling, having been here longer than I care to recount, although not as long as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that setting up another piece of bureaucratic-machinery in the form of an administrative review board would not be satisfactory.
Such action would not take into account the actual operations of bureaucracy and of similar organizations in our society today. This comment is valid not only for government bureaucracies, but, as well, for all large organizations, because they all tend to exhibit the same kind of behaviour. For example, the behaviour of a large private organization such as General Motors is not significantly different from that of a bureaucracy connected with a department of the federal civil service or with a provincial government. Bureaucracies tend to operate under very much the same rules of survival. Consequently, it seems to me that the hon. member's proposal for setting up an administrative review board, independent and unpaid, to adjudicate and make decisions, does not take into account the way in which bureaucracies operate.
I refer the hon. member to the studies of C. Northcote Parkinson on the operation of bureaucracies, to the book "Parkinson's Law" and subsequent developments of it, and also to the two invaluable books on the Peter principle. These, I think, are useful in determining the nature of bureaucracy and what can be done about it.

It strikes me that the problems public servants face at this time in this place will not be solved by this bill. Let me give him a brief history.
About two years ago the then minister of manpower and immigration, who is now the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), announced the establishment of the Bryden Commission. Its work culminated in the Bryden report which, due to the interposition of an election and other matters, was never seriously acted on by the government. That report was never presented, mainly because by the time it came out it was considered to be out of date. The president of the Public Service Alliance asked the government not to proceed with it and the government acceded to the wishes of the union as well as to the wishes of its own management side, which in this case I believe was Treasury Board and the Public Service Commission. That study is in the process of being carried on. A time limit has been put on it.
It is anticipated that following our summer recess, if we ever have a recess, this matter will be brought forward and legislation, if required, will be introduced in the House of Commons. So this matter has been under consideration by the government and two studies have been undertaken. The co-operation of the various public service unions is being sought as well as input from the management side. Attempts are being made to understand the problems connected with this delicate subject, and perhaps some time in the fall there will be an opportunity for some committee of the House of Commons to carry out a study of its own, if that is felt necessary. As a result legislation would be introduced by the government to clarify some of the difficulties which have arisen in what I suggest is the trend setting legislation passed in 1966.
The federal government was the first government in Canada to provide union representation to its employees. In working out this new system and developing the new relationships, moving from a paternalistic relationship to a relationship based on equality, there were difficulties. However, progress has been made and we are headed in the right way. I do not believe the solution to this problem lies within the confines of Bill C-36. I wonder if it would be appropriate to have such an agency or review board in areas of employer-employee relationships for Crown corporations. external review. The answer is to get at the root of the problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I had just disposed of some of the arguments put forward by abolitionists against capital punishment and, therefore, against the amendment we are now considering. As one who supports the amendment, I wish to reflect for a moment on the attitude on society toward this proposal, as I see it.
Many members send questionnaires to their constituencies. They receive thousands of replies. I have yet to hear of one member receiving replies the majority of which were opposed to capital punishment. I have not sent out a questionnaire, but I can tell from the hundreds of letters I have received from my constituents that the overwhelming majority of people there favour the retention of capital punishment, and presumably therefore, they would favour the amendment we are considering.
These people know there are problems within the penal system and they recognize that a swift solution is not possible. But they want us to take a step in that direction, and the first thing they want is a return to capital punishment, for whatever value it has. I have already dealt with this aspect. I am certain they would support the amendment because it is a step in the direction of returning to society some of the conditions we enjoyed when we felt easy about walking around in our neighbourhoods and in our own ridings without worrying about what would happen to us.
Society as a whole has a responsibility not only to rehabilitate criminals and murderers but toward the innocent masses of society who are being inconvenienced, frightened-there are any number of words we could use to describe the conditions which exist. There is a quotation which I thought worth mentioning, taken from an article written on this topic.
Perhaps convicted murderers are not fit to live in our society and rather than imprison them with its care and menace-
They are interesting words-"care" and "menace".
-better to kill them and be done with it.
If a man is not fit to live in society I think society owes it to the people to rid society of that man. I do not intend to get into the life imprisonment angle, but it has been said that this could be a worse punishment than being executed.
There is another aspect which is overlooked when we talk about the innocent masses. It is the type of protection they need. This sentence illustrates it well:
Some people may take the law Into their own hands if they think the state will not. If a man knows his wife's murderer will serve only seven years in prison for the crime he may be inclined, and understandably so, to execute the man himself and serve the seven years in place of his wife's killer.
I have said this before. The innocent who suffer as a result of a murder deserve the protection of society and of the law. There is always a danger that these innocents will take the law into their own hands in other ways and form vigilante or other undesirable groups. The people in my riding want safety in the streets for themselves and for their families. They are very much aware that some of the laws are too lax and that enforcement is too lax. They

think of places like New York city, which perhaps at one time was a pleasant place to visit and walk around at night but where now not only do you not dare go out at night but you find hardly any people living there, it is such a dreadful place. The people in my riding want to know there are certain rules which will be enforced. They think society needs to be saved from itself. They think we can save society by restoring, among other things, capital punishment, which would implement the amendment we are talking about in respect of murder resulting from rape.
The people cannot understand why parliamentarians, at least the abolitionists, apparently reject the view of the law enforcement agencies all over the country, if not all over the world, that there should be a return to capital punishment for this sort of offence. A return to law and order is wanted by all these people and they have made their views known to me. I do not have any difficulty agreeing with the view of the majority of my constitu-tents. I think this is still a democracy. The people think this too. They know the majority of Canadians are in favour of capital punishment and in favour of this kind of amendment. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now at the report stage of Bill C-2, an act concerning capital punishment. In order to make this act still more effective, the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) has moved an amendment incorporating into the bill the case of murders which might be considered as punishable by death.
For the past five years, the government-as far as I know, it is the same old gang-has wanted the abolition of capital punishment for all murders except that of a police officer or prison guard.
For the past five years, we have constantly been hearing about murders of women as well as men, young as well as elderly people, policemen and prison guards as well as ordinary individuals. With such a sampling, we are therefore able to analyze the situation, to probe files, to turn everything upside down in order to find out whether, under the act, punishment has been dealt out or better still, whether the law has simply been applied.
I surely need not discourse any longer to convince the House that in spite of the law passed by Parliament, in no case did we respect our commitments towards society. Policemen have been killed. Did we, as the law stipulates, punish the murderers with death? No. So why should we waste our time enacting laws if we are the first to ignore them? And then, we expect the people to enforce the laws we pass.
Mr. Speaker, the past is the guarantee of the future, and despite what some government members may say, even if we should pass some law or other, we know in advance they will not enforce it. The government is using Bill C-2 to play politics, to play blackmail politics, to try to convince the people that we, federal members, work hard at serious problems.

What difference is there, Mr. Speaker, between discussing and studying this bill on July 24th and discussing it on November 24th? We know ahead of time that it will never be enforced. But to play politics, the government wants to compel the opposition parties to pass bills at full speed before the summer recess.
That is simply the petty method used by the government not to legislate according to the will of the people, but to threaten opposition parties and try, as I said, to railroad bills as loony, frivolous and thoughtless as the one now before the House.
Yet, throughout Canada, surveys have shown clearly- surveys conducted both by members of Parliament and agencies without political allegiance-that most people are calling for the restoration of capital punishment, and that, because society wants to be protected.
In spite of this consensus, the government, the Liberal party wants at all costs and without delay to force Parliament to pass a legislation which goes against the wishes of the majority.
In my riding, 82 per cent of the people are in favour of retaining capital punishment for premeditated murders and not only for people who murder police officers and prison guards or, according to the amendment under review, for people who kill a woman after raping her.
We favour this amendment because, first, it demonstrates the stupidity of the government, second, it widens the concept of the protection of society. I say "the stupidity of the government" because if a man kills a woman after raping her, they want to punish him by death, but the case of a woman who would kill a man in the same situation is not provided for in the amendment. She will probably be commended for such an achievement. If a homosexual attacks a man and kills him while raping him, fine, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has had a law passed that legalized homosexuality. Therefore, no capital punishment for this privileged race, unless obviously it is discovered afterwards, and here I am interpreting the legislation, that the victim of the murder was a police officer or a prison guard. Then according to the law the murderer is punishable by death even though in effect this is not enforced. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) does not, for one, comply with the legislation that he and his colleagues pass in the House.
Mr. Speaker, here is another example. If a woman rapes a young boy who dies from it, no capital punishment because the murderer was a woman. These are the terms of the amendment. If a man rapes a girl-I do not know if the word "woman" implies any segregation between unmarried and married girls-he is sentenced to death. We could give many such examples, but I will only mention that murder is punishable by capital punishment whether carried out during or after the rape. Culpability also depends on the victim's sex and occupation.
A skilled gangster should choose his victim carefully and however ridiculous it may seem, he should kill the Prime Minister's wife rather than a woman who is member of the police force. He should make sure to rape her only after her death, because if he did so before it could cost him his life. After all, if he kills her before
July 24, 1973

raping her, I doubt that there has been a rape, since the victim was unable to spurn or yield to the advances of the criminal.
So many fine distinctions, so many ways to amuse the lawyers. And I point out in this House that those same lawyers are divided, some being for the death penalty, others against it. However, they have all studied the same laws, but they realize how important it is to complicate them, because their daily bread is involved. Indeed, they can be pleased, because they are assured of obtaining more interesting cases than those they now have.
Mr. Speaker, the people refuse to become the plaything of gloomy politicians such as those who hold power. People want laws to be respected and law-abiding individuals to be protected.
Not only do the government and its departments not respect the laws established by Parliament, but what is even worse, they encourage those who unhappily do not abide by the laws.

Mr. Speaker, it is precisely the motion I was talking about when I indicated the segregations the amendment seems to introduce in the bill. It would be against the wishes of the people who would like to see an amendment which would reestablish capital punishment not out of segregation but in a general way for all murders premeditated or not.
Then, in this perspective, we have to consider that the system as a whole which supposes compliance with the laws, as we see now, does not seem to afford individuals the protection they have a right to expect and this to the extent that we see-and we saw it this year-murderers or outlaws, prisoners get the permission to entertain themselves, to go and see hockey games at the Montreal Forum. On the other hand, we never heard that unhappy, miserable people, those who live on welfare, could get tickets from the government to entertain themselves and see hockey games too.
I was saying that somehow the government favours those people who do not comply with the laws. The poor people are never that lucky; on the contrary, they are penalized. But murderers must be rewarded; after all, a good hockey game or a walk through the Salon de la
Capital Punishment
Femme is probably a reward for getting rid of a future welfare recipient.
To show you the extent of our leaders' madness, Mr. Speaker, I would go so far as to say that I know a good many cases of unhappy, but law abiding people, depending on social welfare, who are not entitled to any recreational activities. If, by any chance, they own a car, their allowance is withdrawn and they are told to sell their car, often an old jalopy, worth about $50, if they want their cheque. On the other hand, the same people on social welfare are not entitled to get out of their misery or to be entertained; but a bandit, in short a smart bandit who infringes the law, is rewarded. Not only he is entitled to an automobile to go to his recreational activities, but he is provided with a private chauffer, paid by the state, to be entertained while serving his sentence.
This is the society that our practical jokers, our leaders, are building for us; on the one hand, by legalizing murder of an innocent, of a child, and on the other hand, by rewarding the murderer of an individual. It is with this kind of position that the government wants to obtain a "just society".
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that not only is the present act unfair but it is discriminatory in respect of those who do abide by the law. This government seems to want to say, go ahead, ladies and gentlemen, kill, you will be rewarded for having contributed to solving the alleged problem of overpopulation. But before you kill, make sure that the man is neither a policeman nor a prison guard, or if you prefer to kill a woman make sure that it is not in the course of making love and also that she is neither a policewoman nor a prison guard because that would cost you your head. And, finally, go ahead, kill anybody, anywhere, anytime, because the law will not really be applied as has been seen in the past.
The Prime Minister undoubtedly prefers to listen to the demands of those sentenced to death for murder than listen to society which suffers from insecurity. We have seen enough people thus sentenced to death, blessed people who will have three meals a day for the rest of their lives, watch colour television, occasionally attend sporting events at the expense of the state and finally be released with the blessing of the right hon. government of Canada.
In conclusion, I simply want to ask those responsible both for the bill and the amendment to stop looking at themselves as angels and be human with everything that that entails, that is respecting those individuals who respect their fellow individuals. Then we will see legislation to protect society and not wrongdoers. We will see the restoration of capital punishment for all capital murders without any restriction of segregation and we will thus contribute to protecting society. After all, Mr. Speaker, that is our role and the approach people expect from us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this occasion to speak in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin). Basically, her amendment makes sense to me. It suggests that persons who deliberately commit an act which results in the

July 24, 1973
Capital Punishment
death of another person shall be punished by death. That makes sense to me and to many people across Canada. While I do not wish to belabour the matter of the sentence of death and whether or not society has the right to punish the guilty in this way, this is the supreme test of those who are chosen to govern society, namely, whether or not they can take it upon themselves to adjudicate or to rule in authority in the case of acts of violence or acts against society.
The hon. member's amendment suggests that anyone caught and charged with this offence may be subject to the supreme penalty. In saying this I am not necessarily saying that I am absolutely in favour of that supreme penalty. I think as legislators we could devise a better system than hanging for the taking of the lives of violators. But that is not the point now before the House of Commons. The question before the House is the hon. member's amendment, and we must address ourselves to it.
Under the present law one who commits premeditated murder is charged with what is commonly called capital murder. One who causes a death as a result of anger, jealousy, or other emotional outburst, just on the spur of the moment, is charged with non-capital murder. In the hon. member's amendment we have a further clarification or differentiation between capital murder and non-capital murder.
The hon. member's amendment suggests that anyone convicted of rape and murder be subjected to capital punishment. Under such circumstances, I could agree with the hon. member. But I have seen the opposite argued, that rape cannot be committed without consent. I do not necessarily believe that. Rape is a supreme example of wanton pilferage. We have seen many examples of it in the country of our neighbours to the south.
What is society doing to protect itself? In suburbia we see housewives arming themselves with pistols, or some other means of defence against what could be called wanton pilferage. If as legislators we allow the law enforcement agencies in our society to become engaged solely in reprimanding the persons caught, this is not at all sufficient. We have to go one step further. We must caution people in society that they cannot do certain actions.
I do not know how many hon. members have been reading the newspapers in recent days, but from reports in them I have no hesitation in suggesting that the occurrence of rape in Toronto, Montreal and in the west has been on the increase. One must ask why. Is it because of a lack of appreciation of the judicial system? I think more severe penalties should be imposed on people who deliberately take advantage of others unable to defend themselves.
Some two or three weeks ago the attention of the House of Commons was directed to the bludgeoning to death of an 82 year old lady in the city of Edmonton, Alberta. She lived in an apartment house and had refused to hand over her money. That is not an uncommon thing. The people who broke into her apartment did not know her age. They thought the most they faced was a couple of months in jail for committing burglary.
(Mr. Horner (Crowfoot).]
The same thing happened to an elderly lady of 78 or 79 years in the city of Calgary. I do not think Alberta is different from the rest of Canada in this respect. I may be accused of being hypersensitive to incidents in the province of Alberta, but from my reading of the press I believe such incidents are increasing all across Canada-in Montreal, in Quebec, in Toronto, in Vancouver, and even in the Maritimes. From studying newspapers and RCMP reports one could discover the exact statistics. One must ask why these break-ins took place. Were these elderly ladies bludgeoned to death merely that others could steal the money they had received as pensions? No, I really do not think so. They were break-ins committed by those desirous of some other extreme pleasures, which some people take upon themselves and which I do not think society appreciates happen. I think this House of Commons should recognize the fact that 70 per cent of the people of Canada seriously doubt that a murderer today really takes into consideration the ultimate penalty for his crime. Why do those people committing the ultimate crime not take into consideration the desire of most of the people of Canada? It is because of loss of confidence in the judicial system in our country.
This is a sad thing in this day and age, a time when we in Canada throw out our chests and boast of our educational system, and how knowledgeable we are in understanding one another and of the comprehensive desires of the individual. It is a sad thing in an educated society today that most of the people that commit the ultimate crime have no confidence whatsoever in the judicial system. They say "I know a deliberate murder will not result in my receiving the death penalty; I will serve X number of years and then I will go scot free, so why should I worry?"
It is a strange situation when we reach that degree of misunderstanding within the educated society in which we are living. One would think the direct opposite, Mr. Speaker, was true. One would think that in an educated society those people committing the crime would really believe they would pay the penalty, but the direct converse is true.
I think this is a question which the governing power should answer, the governing power being that body which is putting forward this bill which will continue the so-called experiment. The governing body is putting forward this experiment. There is no question about this issue in the minds of the Canadian people; Gallup poll results suggest that 70 per cent or 80 per cent, whichever figure you want to relate to, are in favour of obtaining the death penalty. Among the urban people it is 80 per cent and among the rural people it is 85 per cent, and I suppose, being a Conservative, I have to say it is 70 per cent, because playing it safe is part of my nature. But certainly between 70 per cent and 85 per cent of the people of Canada believe that we must retain in our society an effective system of capital punishment.
How effective should capital punishment be? The bill before the House of Commons suggests it should be effective in the case of one committing a murder of a police officer or a prison guard. As a representative of a fair percentage of Canadian voters, I suggest that perhaps that
July 24, 1973

does not go far enough. I do not necessarily believe that all murderers should have their sentences commuted; neither do I necessarily believe that all murderers should be hanged. But I do believe there should be degrees, that there should be qualifying factors.
Now, with murder with intent I am in no trouble. In cases of murder with a degree of deliberation to involve the death of a certain person there is no question in my mind that the person who commits that murder, or who orders the death of that person, should be committed to death himself. I have no question in my mind about that, no qualms, no loss of sleep. I know many solicitors general, Mr. Speaker, who have found that question a problem.
How much further do we go? Capital Punishment
we are acknowledging that the previous five-year trial period was not successful in the eyes of the majority of Canadians. Therefore, another trial ban must distinguish in better fashion between those crimes which are capital crimes and those crimes which are not. We may find that partial ban legislation, which defines murder-rapes and kidnap-murders as capital crimes, will assure Canadians of the security and safety to which they have a right. We may find after five years that we still have not gone far enough. But to refrain from including this amendment in the bill would be a forfeiture by this Parliament of its primary duty, that of serving Canadians.
Rape and kidnapping are two terrible crimes which, according to statistics and news reports, are increasing at an alarming rate. The figures have been quoted previously by other speakers and I do not need to repeat them. They are particularly terrible because they damage the moral and mental fibre of the victims and persons close to the victims. The terror and anguish which is experienced as a result of these crimes is something which no person should have to endure. On these grounds alone, rape and kidnapping should be recognized as capital crimes.
The amendment does not go as far as that. It requires that a murder be committed as well as a rape or a kidnapping. While I would be in favour of stiffer legislation, I am prepared to accept this amendment as it stands because it will in all likelihood act as a deterrent to potential criminals. All too often the threat of murder is an important factor in these crimes. And all too often death is the result of these crimes. If a criminal knows that murder, in conjunction with either rape or kidnapping, is punishable by death, he may have second thoughts about committing the crimes at all.
I do not accept those arguments which claim that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent to murder. Proponents of this theory overlook the impact that the threat of execution has on all criminals who carry a weapon, whether they be professional killers or milk store bandits. Many prisoners spoke freely of using unloaded weapons prior to the temporary ban on capital punishment, but they spoke just as freely of loading those guns after the ban went into effect. These feelings are common to most criminals.
The amendment suggests that members of parliament are aware of the need for deterrents with respect to certain crimes. Murder as a result of kidnapping or rape is certainly a crime for which deterrents are needed.
It is difficult to enter into a discussion of this amendment without straying into a more general discussion of abolition or retention of capital punishment. At the risk of straying, I would like to say that I do hope this amendment signifies a trend toward developing a safer society for Canadians. Is murder as a result of rape or kidnapping any more final than murder as a result of other premeditated crimes? How can we construct a partition between, for example, the acts of a kidnapper and the acts of a thief who murders a storekeeper? Both crimes contain elements of planning and strategy. Both involve the possibility of death. The need for a crackdown in law enforcement is recognized by most Canadians. Our entire society is jeopardized by weak laws, especially as they apply to the maintenance of society.

While I respect the legal sagacity and experience of the hon. member for St. Catharines before the criminal courts of this land, I do not back off from him because of that. While I have not defended a murderer, I have certainly defended many people who were alleged to have committed rape.
I certainly admire and respect the fortitude it must have taken for the hon. lady to move this amendment. If the government had any doubt about the strong feeling on the basic issue in the bill before us, it can have no doubt left after the strong debate the first amendment has evoked. Look at the deep-felt and sincere emotion of my hon.
Capital Punishment
friend from St. Catharines (Mr. Morgan), who asked the House some rhetorical questions which may be hard to answer. When my friend asks, Mr. Speaker, how one can have respect for the law when there is no respect for life, I turn to him and ask in return: How do you have respect for the law when there is no penalty befitting the crime? I say to my friend: How is it that you have respect for the law when there is no sanction in the sentence?
And my friend questions again: How can you believe in capital punishment when you have, or should have, a reverence for life? I am sure my friend did not intend to infer that any member of this House, regardless of the strength of his feelings on the issue of capital punishment, has any diluted reverence for life. I want to assure him that I have as deep a reverence for life as any member of this House, and because I feel this great sense of reverence for life I respect people and believe that the ultimate crime should be met by capital punishment after all the due processes of law have been followed. The case of Tanya Bush is the incident which finally swung my opinion from abolition to retention.
Three times, Mr. Speaker, in the seven year period in which I have been a member the House has been confronted with the fundamental issue here, life, or the philosophy of life, the poetry of idealism or the actuality of reality. None of us want to pull the door that makes someone lose his life, but I say that the House of Commons, regardless of public opinion, cannot get lost in philosophic homilies and beautiful platitudes which we would love to believe. The state takes life every time there is a war. War is a crime against society. I say murder is a crime. I say murder is a war against an individual, and because it is a war against an individual after due process of law the potential ultimate sanction should be there in our rule books.
We all know that armed with the power to exercise executive clemency, or the Royal prerogative of mercy, this government, if it stays in power, is not going to follow the law. They have not followed the law since it has been in the books. Because of reverence for life, because of respect for people, the House of Commons must discharge its responsibility too, in the most reprehensible of situations.
My friend, a learned criminal lawyer, fully knows the facts on Tanya Bush. And they fit directly into the amendment of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin). Three child killings and then while the culprit is out on weekend leave from a penitentiary, because he has a grudge against Tanya Bush's father, he kills Tanya Bush who is eight or nine years old. Four child killings, three girls and one boy.
I have four children, Mr. Speaker, and I am not going to get overly emotional about this, but it is because I have a reverence for life and a respect for life, and because I do not want a Tanya Bush situation to repeat itself, that I have no hesitation about voting for this amendment, which at least extends the principle of capital punishment up to a point.
To follow my friend's argument to a conclusion, he says there is no logic to this debate; and he is right, Mr. Speaker. The issue of capital punishment is one which evokes the primary instincts of everybody, and that is

Capital Punishment
why I do not think there is an issue since I have been a member of parliament which has sustained the interest of so many people from my constituency and from coast to coast. I agree with many of my friends and certain of the abolitionists up to a point; statistics do not mean anything in this debate. That is why you can walk into a barber shop, into a cocktail party, into a constituency meeting or into a church, and once the business is over the question comes up: What are you going to do about capital punishment? You do not need facts to cloud the issue. It is instinctive, as I say. It goes to the fundamentals of life, and that, basically, is simple.
If you follow what my friend says, that because the crime is so reprehensible in the case of rape that the fellow must be so sick that he ought not to be punished too severely. Where do we find ourselves? Pierre Laporte lost his life two and a half to three years ago. One man has been sentenced, I think, for his murder. No one has been faced with the ultimate penalty. No one has been hanged because of that heinous incident, that blot on our history.
If we were talking about the situation 50 years ago or even 25 years ago, I would most likely have joined those who were urging us to move forward. But the balance has shifted and as the hon. member from Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) said the other night, provoking an angry response from the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), there is too little concern for the victims of these heinous crimes. I have listened to speeches, as I say, for the last seven years telling us that capital punishment is not a deterrent. But, Mr. Speaker, those statistics are only developed on the basis of those who have committed crimes. I agree it is most likely you cannot prove the contrary, but who knows what goes through the mind of someone who has a grudge, or wants to exceed all reasonable conduct. If there was a capital penalty, he might just not carry out the offence he contemplates.
Look at our jails. We are talking about prison guards and prison treatment. There is a higher rate of killings in the jails, if my reading of the newspapers is correct, than there is on the streets. This always happened to a degree. There are always grudges in penal institutions and undoubtedly some will go to extremes. But I think such crimes have been increasing, and they can increase with impunity. Because if a man has been sent to jail for life, what has he to lose under the present system? Do you want to put a man in a cage for the rest of his life? If he has committed an unfortunate crime, do you want to put him in a cage and leave him there for his natural life? I cannot get caught up on that argument. I think that with our penal system, our parole system and proper safeguards for those who commit the ultimate crime, there still should be a process of proper review. But I say the heinous crime, the repeated crime, the crime under contract, out to kill, the organized crime, comes into a different category.
It is difficult, Mr. Speaker, to stay calm in this debate. We have had a five-year trial period in theory, but it has not been followed in practice. I could go on and get a little political, but my time is running out and we are debating this issue for the third time in seven years.
Ironically, there are some members interested in family allowances, which is at the opposite pole of the capital punishment debate, I suppose. If you are going to deal

with capital punishment on one side, why should you not be thinking about the children of the world, the family allowance situation and the social security situation?
We have heard about high taxes, election expenses, foreign takeovers, crop insurance, mortgage money to help people get homes, and we have heard about the Olympics in Montreal in 1976. We have all these matters to deal with yet we keep this House going all summer on this matter of capital punishment. I hope the research people will dig up the number of days this and the previous Parliament spent on this issue. I do not think half the people of Canada know we are in session and I do not believe the other half care. However, the priorities of this government are twisted. I shall not belabour that point.
I think the government and some of the leaders of all parties have fatally underestimated the deeply held feelings on this issue. Why should we be in session debating this eternal question at this time? Some people may think we should be having a summer recess because we are not dealing with some issues of higher priority. What priority has capital punishment? We have not followed the law for the past five or six years. Is there any more guarantee that we will follow even the sham law, as it was described by my friend from St. Catharines, in the next five years?
This is supposed to be a priority item through the summer recess. It is not really. To show how unreal it is, people in the outside world are still going to cottages. We are elected to look at the evidence in every case, whether it is capital punishment, taxation, or any other matter. We are elected to look at the evidence, to consider the wellbeing of mankind, including our constituents, and to make an honest decision.
If after four or five years the people in my constituency, or indeed any constituency in the country, think we have done a bad job, they have the right and duty to throw us out of office. But if they consider perhaps that some of us in the House, and indeed I hope most of us, try to act in good conscience on the basis of evidence, I have enough faith in the democratic process to believe that there will be members in every political party, including the Social Credit party, who will take what I regard to be the correct stand; and the people in their constituencies, whether or not the majority at this time happens to agree, will respect the honesty and integrity of that decision. I think it is a bastardization, if I can use that term, of the theory of democracy as we know it and have practised it in the British Commonwealth and elsewhere for over 100 years to say that all a responsible politician does is do a Gallup poll in his riding and respond to that. That would not make a good member of parliament, and I do not hesitate to say that.
I have gone through the four arguments presented by the hon. member who preceded me and, as I said, I feel strongly about this because I believe that human life is very important and that neither the state nor any individual has the right to take it. I conclude by saying that if the hon. member accepts my comments regarding his arguments, the only thing he has left is the emotional
|Mr. Broadbent.]
feeling of vengeance. Then he has to say regarding capital punishment; I believe it is right to take the life of another human being just because I feel vindictive. Vindictiveness is no foundation for morality.

The hori. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) pointed out last evening that in her amendment murder combined with rape and kidnapping is a form of premeditated murder, because obviously murder follows the other act.
