subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST THAT MEASURES BE TAKEN TO AVOID ACCIDENTS WHICH RESULT IN DROWNINGS
TRANSPORT-REQUEST THAT MEASURES BE TAKEN TO AVOID ACCIDENTS WHICH RESULT IN DROWNINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 4 I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) if he was aware of the mounting number of tragic summer accidents which result in drownings in the Great Lakes, the Trent canal and other waters of Canada. If so, was he prepared to take the necessary steps to halt this appalling loss of life? The minister replied by saying that we are doing all we can.
One of the reasons, perhaps the most important reason, for my bringing this up is that quite recently a new houseboat, supposedly built by experts, floundered. It sank within a few feet of the dock with the loss of two lives. This boat was supposedly built by expert builders. Why did it go down? This is merely one example of the sort of thing I mean, and I do not intend putting cases on the record that all of us know about.
Over and over again we see tragedies that shock and disturb the whole community. Last season a boat set out from the shore of one of the Great Lakes. There were nine people in it. It was overloaded, the gunwales being almost down to the water line. It sank about half a mile out with the loss of all but two.
I ask, is it not about time we did something about this problem? The responsibilities of the federal government are serious enough. It should take a close look at this area. Are wharf users supervised? Are they told to use certain areas? Are inspectors appointed in all congested boating areas? What inspections are made of boats before they go in the water? Is instruction given, and is education available in this area?
Of all forms of accidental death, drowning ranks third, surpassed only by motor vehicle accidents and falls. As you know, Mr. Speaker, motor vehicle accidents on highways maim over 500,000 people a year on the roads of North America. Those accidents kill over 5,000 people in Canada. Drowning comes next but one in importance as a
Adjournmen t Deba te
cause of death. It is interesting to note that 88 per cent of drowning accidents involve males, that of total male drownings, 44 per cent involve males under 20 years of age, and a further 33 per cent involve males who are between 20 and 40 years old. Among young people of school age, between 4 and 24 years of age, accidents claim far more deaths than all kinds of diseases combined. In this age group motor vehicle accidents rank as the leading cause of death, and drownings rank next as the cause of death.
Taking the normal life expectancy of these young drowning victims as 70 years, their deaths represent a combined loss of nearly 60,000 man years. The male-female sex ratio of drowning victims in these ages was less than seven to one-that is, seven males drowning to one female-compared with a ratio of over 13 to one for ages over 24. Canada's record of drownings at 6.5 per 100,000 of population is substantially higher than that of either the United States or Great Britain. Twice the number of people per capita drown in this country as compared with England, and our drowning ratio is 50 per cent greater than that of the United States. While drownings occur every month of the year in Canada, they appear to be most heavily concentrated in the couple of months of summer recreational activity and annual vacations, when more people go on our waterways. On the other hand, in England and in much of the United States, people can swim 12 months of the year.
Three quarters of the fatalities were due to unexpected submersion. That means that the people involved were thrown into the water. This may have happened because of boating mishaps and falls. Only one fifth of drownings occurred as a result of voluntary submersion involving swimming, wading and diving. That shows that where lifeguards supervise the accident rate has been much improved. Small boat accidents account for 31 per cent of all victims.
The greatest factor in drownings involved falls into rivers. This hazard caused 25 per cent of the drownings. Accidents while wading, diving, etc. were responsible for 20 per cent of all drownings, and 47 per cent of drownings involve the age group between 15 and 19. In 90 per cent of the cases a male was involved, females comprising only 10 per cent, and two thirds of those girls were under 15 years of age. Falls into rivers and lakes constituted one of the greatest hazards for the pre-school age group in which girls accounted for about one fifth of drownings. Swimming accidents in the 5 to 14 year age group accounted for nearly a third of drownings. Falls into lakes and rivers claimed the next largest group of victims, and ice accidents were a particular hazard for this group.
In the age group beyond 50 years, males predominated by more than ten to one in involvement in accidents; accidents in small boats were almost as frequent and accounted for a third of drowning fatalities in this age group.
You will see by these statistics, Mr. Speaker, that younger people make up the bulk of all those involved in accidents in the water. Many are in their most productive years or are just approaching those years. It is for this reason, regardless of who is responsible, that I want to see action taken. Certainly the federal government is liable on

July 24, 1973
Adjournment Debate
the international and federal-provincial waterways and on its own canal system. We need more accurate reports of all water accidents, a study on how to cut this loss and the funds with which to do it.
I hope the minister will have something definite on this. He said he was working on it. I hope he has something to tell us. The minister will say there are certain written laws governing boating and equipment, but are inspections made regularly? The law may be there, but is it being respected?

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST THAT MEASURES BE TAKEN TO AVOID ACCIDENTS WHICH RESULT IN DROWNINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Ministry of Transport regulates pleasure craft by means of the small vessel regulations which set forth the mandatory requirements for life saving and fire fighting equipment. They also make mandatory the affixing of a Ministry of Transport load and horsepower capacity plate which sets out recommended maximums for normal boat operation on any outboard motor not exceeding 16 feet in length powered by a motor of 10 h.p. or more. Provision is made in the regulations for enforcement by peace officers.
The boating restriction regulations provide a means whereby a local government or authority may initiate action through a provincial government to have a formal request from a provincial authority made to the federal government to have a restriction imposed on a given body or area of water. The purpose of the regulations is to prohibit or restrict some or all types of boating activity on the waters specified. It has the very great advantage of having all local differences of opinion sorted out before the province concerned makes formal application to the federal government to have a restriction or prohibition imposed.
The Ministry of Transport approves small vessel lifejackets on the basis of the requirements set forth by the lifejacket committee of the Canadian government specifications board. One of the requirements of this ministry is that every ministry-approved small vessel lifejacket sold be accompanied by the ministry publication "Your Lifejacket," which sets out advice in both official languages on the care and usage of lifejackets.
In an effort to inform the boating public and to alert them to the necessity for safe boating procedures, the ministry publishes and circulates free of charge the pamphlet "Boating Safety Guide". This is published in both official languages and circulation this year has passed the
500,000	mark.
In addition to the foregoing, there are penalties provided in section 240 of the Criminal Code of Canada for operating a boat in a hazardous manner, operating a boat under the influence of alcohol or drugs, towing a water skier during the hours of darkness or without having an observer in the boat.
The ministry is in the process of developing standards for the safe construction of pleasure craft. This is being done in consultation with industry with a view to making such construction standards mandatory. An ongoing program of liaison, public speaking and information dissemination is carried out by the coast guard rescue officer at Trenton with a view to encouraging the safe operation of pleasure and commercial craft. A rescue co-ordination
| Mr. Rynard.]
centre is maintained at Trenton, Ontario, which has as one of its tasks the co-ordination of marine search and rescue operations. This centre is manned jointly by Canadian Armed Forces and Canadian coastguard personnel on a 24 hour per day, seven day week, basis.
The Canadian coastguard operates three primary search and rescue cutters, the Spray, Spume and Spindrift, on the Great Lakes. In addition, the coastguard operates numerous other vessels that are also available to respond quickly to search and rescue missions. The possibility of reactivating an "R" class search and rescue cutter for service on the lakes is being investigated at this time.
An equipment evaluation program is taking place this summer with a view to expanding the trial program of inshore rescue boats introduced with great success last year on the Pacific coast.

REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NORTHERN ONTARIO-JOINT ACTION WITH PROVINCE TO FORMULATE CO-ORDINATED DEVELOPMENT PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 4 last I asked the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) what action for co-ordinated federal-provincial planning was being taken to promote the economic development of northern Ontario, especially the development of secondary industry. I also asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) this question:
Bearing in mind that a DREE report said . . . that thousands of jobs would be lost in northern Ontario due to redundancy in the next few years, what immediate steps will be taken to prevent such an economic upheaval in our area?
The parliamentary secretary said studies were under way, and blamed the province of Ontario for lack of development in the north. The Prime Minister gave a vague reply to the effect that developments were taking place.
Today marks the opening of the conference between the western premiers and the federal government on the subject of the economic alienation of the west. I am gratified to see that the Prime Minister has finally discovered the west and admitted that the development of the west has been neglected by the federal government. Indeed, as the Prime Minister said, the role of the west as primarily a supplier of raw material is over. I hope the Prime Minister will also discover northern Ontario, for we have been for decades suppliers of raw materials with the result that people in our part of the province have been unable to find jobs in secondary industry. I hope the Prime Minister can make the same promise to us in the north and assure us that we will no longer be merely suppliers of raw materials for the heartland of Ontario.
We have been hewers of wood and drawers of water for too long. We have exported our pulp, our iron ore, our minerals, and in doing so we have exported jobs. Between 1966 and 1971 the population of northern Ontario showed a net gain of only 886 people. Between 1965 and 1969 only 14 new manufacturing plants were established in the whole of northern Ontario, employing 527 people. Contrast this with what has happened in the southern part of the prov-
July 24, 1973

ince. Over half of all the new manufacturing capacity has gone there, and in a three year period the population increased by almost half a million people.
It seems to me the federal government has failed in its DREE program to take into account the relationship between the south and the north of this province. I find its working paper, its report, to be a very shallow one, much of it already outdated, particularly with reference to the Abitibi Pulp and Paper plant in Sault Ste. Marie. No reference is made to the fundamental problem in northern Ontario, the failure of federal and provincial governments in the past to do more than provide incentives for northern development. This is the old carrot and stick approach carried out by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Northern Ontario Development Corporation and other agencies, both federal and provincial. We must move beyond this idea of merely giving incentives to the north and adopt a co-ordinated plan of development. We need incentives in the north, but there should also be disincentives to discourage industry locating in the golden horseshoe. In the absence of such disincentives the advantages of locating in the south will always outweigh the attractions of the north, no matter how many incentive programs apply in northern Ontario.
There is need for a comprehensive examination of transportation costs. I might mention that Simpsons-Sears and Eaton's put out two catalogues, one for the south and one for the north. We have to pay between $5 and $20 more than is paid in the south for identical products because of the extra cost of freight. There is need for a complete reassessment of the schedule of rates which discriminate against northern Ontario. A Crown development corporation should be established to co-ordinate plans and promote industry through the expenditure of government funds in the north similar to the arrangement which has been set up in the Maritimes.
Attention should also be paid to the growth centre concept so that communities may have a chance to develop around cities in the north which have some potential for industrial expansion. A Liberal federal government has in fact failed to promote secondary industry in northern Ontario in the past, and so has a Conservative provincial government. These two governments are acting together and tell us they will come up with a great new plan. I hope both governments will listen to the people of the north such as representatives of the municipalities, industrial commissioners, interested businessmen and labour union people who have some very sound ideas about our problems and what is wrong. We have ideas for the north. We will not be content any longer with mere vague plans and promises. We want action now. I should like a response from the parliamentary secretary concerning what specific action will take place now in northern Ontario.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Prud'homme (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NORTHERN ONTARIO-JOINT ACTION WITH PROVINCE TO FORMULATE CO-ORDINATED DEVELOPMENT PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) did, in fact, ask a question some time ago, to which I replied, and I might very briefly elaborate on the measures which have been taken since then.
As the hon. member is aware, the minister appeared before the parliamentary committee on several occasions.
Adjournment Debate
He announced that he was undertaking a series of consultations with the provincial governments. This was done, and they have now been completed. The various levels of government are in the process of developing the solutions which may be applied to this very serious problem raised by the hon. member.
The report of the various provincial committees was tabled in the House last June; the details on the reorganization of the department were announced to the committee members, and in particular to the employees of the department, on July 5, and the minister has, moreover, been prepared to table the internal management documents since last July 5.
The minister also announced, not only that a regional office will be set up in each of the major centres, such as the Maritimes, Quebec, Ontario and the western provinces, but also that special measures concerning a very special office will be considered, and possibly approved for northern Ontario.
The hon. member pointed out, in his remarks, that the time has now come to act, but in the same breath he said that we need-

If I am quoting the hon. member correctly, I believe he said we need a comprehensive study of transportation rates. The hon. member said we need action now. The hon. member at the same time stated that we need a whole re-assessment; that we need a Crown corporation to study the situation, and at the same time he said we need action now. Then he said we need a new centre concept, and he wants action now.
Needless to say, if we really want to know where we are going we must definitely be sure of what action will be taken. This demands much co-ordination between the provincial government and the federal government. I am not trying to pass the buck, but I must say that much of the responsibility for this is in the hands of the provincial government. In this connection, however, I wholeheartedly agree with the hon. member that not only has the time come for action, but that the time has come to see whether the natural resources of Canada will be sent out of Canada in their raw state or as finished products. This is a major problem not only for northern Ontario but also in respect to natural resources in the province of Quebec and in the western provinces. So I think some action will be taken having in mind the very good words of the hon. member.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-INCREASE IN FREIGHT RATES IN ATLANTIC PROVINCES-POSSIBLE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO OFFSET SERIOUS EFFECTS
TRANSPORT-INCREASE IN FREIGHT RATES IN ATLANTIC PROVINCES-POSSIBLE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO OFFSET SERIOUS EFFECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to raise again the matter of the transportation policy of the federal government in eastern Canada, a subject which has been raised constantly in the chamber over the years and more specifically during the month of June by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) and myself. On June 18, both the hon. member for Hillsborough and I inquired of the minister whether or not he would shortly take action to alleviate the very serious situation with respect to freight rates in the Atlantic

July 24, 1973
Adjournment Debate
provinces. This is a matter with which the minister is not unfamiliar inasmuch as a major delegation of Atlantic premiers plus interested parties approached the minister earlier this year, and at that time the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) gave extensive assurances to them as well as to representatives of major organizations that action would very shortly be taken.
Unfortunately, in recent weeks the Minister of Transport has apparently preferred to shift the burden of responsibility for federal transportation policy to the Atlantic premiers, and to my mind this has been a rather poor effort on his part.
It is somewhat of a coincidence that tonight I have the opportunity again to raise this matter, because just yesterday an announcement was made with respect to transportation in the Atlantic provinces and in Quebec. The announcement-I will not read all of it but only the first few lines which set out the basic aspect-reads in part:
The government of Canada and governments of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Quebec have reached agreement in principle that to assist regional industry the existing westbound Maritime Freight Rates Act and Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act 30 per cent truck and rail subsidies will be augmented for selected commodities. This increase will be subject to existing regulations of the Maritime Freight Rates Act and Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act, and in addition the following conditions are intended . . .
I plan to speak about those conditions for a moment, but I want to comment, first of all, on the basic announcement. The announcement really leaves out more than it includes. The basic question of the extent of the increase above 30 per cent which has operated since 1969 is not defined, and I think this is an incredible omission after this length of time.
In the late 1960s we adopted a new transportation policy, and I think since September of 1969 there have been successive increases which have detrimentally affected the economy of the Atlantic provinces. These increases run to something like eight or nine in number, and the impact extends in a major way to almost 68 per cent in increases in the past four years. Now we are given this announcement by the minister with very little indication of what it will mean to producers in the Atlantic provinces. There is no indication what commodities would benefit or to what degree. There is no indication how much of a rate Increase we can expect. We are simply told that there will be an augmentation of the present one.
Will it significantly close the very large gap that has opened in freight rate increases in the last four years? We are not told. Will it be a token gesture to placate some of the more vociferous elements of the economic community of the Atlantic provinces? We are not told. When will it start? Again there is no indication. Most important of all, who will make the basic decision in terms of the variety of rates and the commodities which will be covered? In terms of the qualifications that are attached to this announcement, we are shown again that there is no willingness to face in a serious way the considerable transportation difficulties that exist in the Atlantic provinces. This is a very selective kind of announcement in that it will only cover one way traffic; that is, outbound western traffic from the Atlantic provinces. It in no way will deal with the very serious problems for manufacturers and processors in the

Atlantic provinces who often must import at very high charge, because of transportation costs, materials and items used in the manufacture of finished products either for distribution and sale in the Atlantic provinces or beyond.
This announcement will not deal with our export situation. This is an incredible admission when you realize that the Atlantic provinces are on the doorstep of major export markets both in Europe as well as in the eastern seaboard region of the United States.
There is no clear-cut assistance, as I said previously, for manufacturing materials. Also there is no grappling with the fundamental problem of what to do with intraregional transportation. This, in addition, will be complicated by the fact that the administration that is likely to be loaded on to the carriers, and to some degree on the shippers, may add to costs. I do not think that matter has been examined in view of the very brief announcement by the minister.
I hope that the parliamentary secretary, in replying this evening, can give us some indication that there will be a much more positive, comprehensive and detailed program announced very shortly. Otherwise the alienation that has been greatly discussed in western Canada will become even more apparent in Atlantic Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: TRANSPORT-INCREASE IN FREIGHT RATES IN ATLANTIC PROVINCES-POSSIBLE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO OFFSET SERIOUS EFFECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, concerning the rate increases, the railways have given notice that they will increase agreed charges for all contracts by 6 per cent. One of the conditions under the law is that these contracts may be terminated by either side on three months written notice. Agreed charges are low contract rates voluntarily agreed to by shippers and railways, in return for which the shippers agree to ship a stated percentage of their traffic by rail.
Shippers who are parties to agreed charges affected by the railways' announcement have the option of agreeing to the higher rates that will be effective September 1, or afterwards, or of withdrawing from the agreed charges, in which case they could ship by rail at open tariff rates, or by another mode such as truck, or ship their goods by their own trucks. But there is no general increase in freight rates anticipated in the Maritimes.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) met on April 9 with the premiers of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island to discuss transportation matters affecting the Atlantic provinces. It was agreed at that meeting that steps should be initiated to increase westbound Atlantic region freight subsidies above the current 30 per cent level on a selective basis, aimed particularly at helping the manufacturing and agricultural industries in that region. It was also jointly agreed that the federal-provincial committee on Atlantic region transportation would begin working out such a program.
While an officer of MOT is chairing the committee, the definition of commodities to qualify for the selective subsidies was made the responsibility of the provincial members of the committee. They felt that they could not draw up this list from their own resources but should consult with local industry.

On June 21 the Minister of Transport announced that the federal-provincial committee was making good progress toward finalizing recommendations for the selective increases. He said that the increases were intended to aid Atlantic region shippers east of Quebec City in reaching the central Canadian market. He said that shippers in the Atlantic region would be notified shortly by public adver-
Adjournment Debate
tisement of the general basis of eligibility under the selectivity criteria being developed, and that they would be invited to submit to their respective provincial governments lists of commodities they wish included in the expanded subsidy program. This process will likely take some time, and at least one or two more committee meetings, before matters are finalized.
